International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose.

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose.

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

Three dynamics have held up reform. But each may be slowly giving way, creating a rare window for genuine change.

The first and most commonly cited obstacle is the Security Council’s five permanent veto-wielding members, or P5—the United States, China, Russia, France, and the United Kingdom. The P5 countries are wary of admitting rising powers as fellow veto wielders, as it would diminish their own influence in the body and make it more susceptible to deadlock.

However, without reform, the council’s legitimacy in the eyes of the global majority will deteriorate, rendering it more and more irrelevant. The P5 will be the biggest losers if the UNSC fades into insignificance, as they have the most to lose: their veto prerogatives. Consequently, the P5 are only likely to allow for reform when the council appears to be nearing the brink of collapse—a point that the world may soon approach if the P5 continue to wield their vetoes with impunity.

The second issue is the deadlock between the two main reform groupings: the G4 coalition of Germany, Japan, Brazil, and India, which favor enlarging the permanent membership of the UNSC to include themselves, and the Uniting for Consensus group, which favors only adding additional elected seats to the council. The uncompromising competition between these two blocs has prevented other proposals from gaining steam. However, Germany’s recent failed bid for a two-year term on the council has put into question the viability of its claim to a permanent seat—and the viability of the G4 proposal as a whole. This enables a possible shake-up that allows for the emergence of new and more creative reform ideas.

The third factor is that discussions over which reform model would best enhance the UNSC’s efficiency, effectiveness, and legitimacy has, to date, been largely speculative. Neither side has been able to predict with any meaningful accuracy the implications of their proposed reforms.

This, too, is now changing. Thanks to artificial intelligence, complex simulations can be conducted that calculate potential shifts in the council’s performance. We have conducted such a simulation to determine precisely what each proposal would achieve—and what it would risk. The simulation shows that the G4 model would dramatically increase gridlock over the next five decades. Council business would slow down as decision-making speed per resolution would grow from 28.5 days to 42.1 days, and veto use would grow by more than 60 percent. Despite giving them a seat at the table, the resulting paralysis would encourage leading powers to work outside the UNSC, defeating the purpose of reform entirely.

Yet while the Uniting for Consensus group’s proposal would limit the damage to the council’s efficiency and effectiveness, it fails to resolve its legitimacy deficit. The UNSC cannot effectively serve as a long-term custodian of the international order if Britain continues to enjoy a more privileged position than India—the world’s most populous country and likely soon to be its third-largest economy.

How, then, to resolve this conundrum? The AI simulation points to two mechanisms.

First, if more countries are to gain the veto, then this must be balanced by creating a veto override mechanism: for example, a veto wielder must secure one or two concurring negative votes among sitting council members, otherwise, a two-thirds majority in the General Assembly can overturn the veto.

The simulation shows that this would reduce veto usage by up to 40 percent, even before any cast vetoes are overturned. It would also speed up decision-making on average from 28.5 days to 21 days because veto wielders would either know that they have the necessary concurring vote(s) and cast their veto without delay, or know that they don’t and be incentivized to compromise to avoid a potentially humiliating General Assembly override.

Skeptics argue that the P5 countries are unlikely to agree to any reform that dilutes their veto privileges. But the simulation projects that successful overrides would occur only 28 percent of the time (or as low as 14 percent of the time, if the vote to override takes place by public roll call rather than by secret ballot). Agreeing to this limited mechanism, which would only take effect when a great power is isolated to the point of having no allies on an expanded council, is a small price to pay to ensure the council’s long-term legitimacy—and the permanent members’ privileged position that comes with it.

Second, a pool of “semipermanent” members, serving multiple lengthy terms and rotating on and off the council a few countries at a time, would offer middle powers that fail to earn a permanent seat a substantial consolation prize. According to the simulation, it would also triple small states’ likelihood of election to an ordinary council seat by taking these middle powers out of the running.

Countries such as Japan, Brazil, Argentina, India, and Pakistan currently monopolize the council’s nonpermanent seats, serving on average more than one term per decade, leaving smaller countries to earn a place only once every 30-50 years. The simulation shows that this proposal, if tabled by a strong coalition of small and developing states, has a 78 percent chance of being adopted and contributing to breaking the logjam.

The “international order” may be an abstract concept, but it takes concrete form in the institutions through which states manage their differences, constrain the use of force, and prevent conflict from descending into chaos. None matters more than the UNSC.

For decades, the presumed trade-off between legitimacy and effectiveness has been an obstacle to meaningful reform. Our simulations suggest that this is a false choice: A more representative council can also be a more effective one. What is, in fact, impossible is a new and stable order without a Security Council designed for it.

Zachary Paikin is the deputy director of the Better Order Project at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

Trita Parsi is the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. X: @tparsi

#5995. Hegseth’s Leadership Has Damaged the Pentagon

Argument: Hegseth’s Leadership Has Damaged the Pentagon

On Monday, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives that could come as early as this week. Massie, a Republican who will leave Congress in January, accuses Hegseth of waging an “unlawful” war in Iran and abusing the office. Hegseth will be the first civilian leader of the U.S. military establishment to face impeachment in 150 years.

The last, William Belknap, was President Ulysses S. Grant’s secretary of war—the title at the time for the civilian leader of the U.S. Army, before a unified Defense Department. The House voted unanimously to impeach him. Belknap resigned ahead of his Senate trial; he avoided conviction because of many senators’ discomfort with impeaching a private citizen. (Impeachments do not require the accused to be in office.)

On Monday, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives that could come as early as this week. Massie, a Republican who will leave Congress in January, accuses Hegseth of waging an “unlawful” war in Iran and abusing the office. Hegseth will be the first civilian leader of the U.S. military establishment to face impeachment in 150 years.

The last, William Belknap, was President Ulysses S. Grant’s secretary of war—the title at the time for the civilian leader of the U.S. Army, before a unified Defense Department. The House voted unanimously to impeach him. Belknap resigned ahead of his Senate trial; he avoided conviction because of many senators’ discomfort with impeaching a private citizen. (Impeachments do not require the accused to be in office.)

Massie’s charge sheet includes eight counts, the most severe of which is that Hegseth “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization” and “demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

Four of the counts of impeachment involve war powers, while the others concern civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings during boat strikes, suppressing free speech, and kidnapping a foreign leader.

The indictment does not include some of Hegseth’s more egregious norm- and law-violating behavior: violating the Impoundment Control Act by refusing to release funds authorized and appropriated by Congress for aid to Ukraine, requiring uniformed military participation in partisan rallies, refusing briefings to congressional Democrats, denying press access to the Pentagon, firing without explanation more than two dozen senior officers confirmed by the Senate in their ranks and positions, appointing people forced out of military service for insubordination or political acts to senior civilian positions in the Defense Department, renaming the department without congressional authorization, and campaigning against sitting members of Congress.

President Donald Trump continues to support Hegseth, praising him for “winning two wars.” And the defense secretary continues undaunted: On Nov. 5, he released a nearly six-minute video insisting that “this is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you’ve noticed, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

The defense secretary’s most important responsibility is managing Congress because under the U.S. Constitution, it is Congress that has the power to “raise and support Armies” and “provide and maintain a Navy.” Hegseth has poisoned those relationships. It is likely that his impeachment will be successful in the House on at least the count of attempting to penalize the speech of Sen. Mark Kelly, whom Hegseth groundlessly accused of sedition. (Hegseth has initiated proceedings to retroactively reduce Kelly’s military rank and retirement pay.)

Rep. James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House oversight committee, sounds dubious about defending Hegseth rather than supportive, saying that “there are a lot of questions” about the defense secretary. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is a “hard yes” on impeachment. Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn appears unlikely to give Hegseth an exit with honor by appointing him to her vacant Senate seat.

Trump will surely goad Hegseth on to fight the impeachment and behave outrageously—both as a distraction from the drubbing of the Republicans in the midterm elections and to indulge his entertainment approach to governance since it would be “great television.”

Whether or not Hegseth is convicted, his actions have already cost the Defense Department years of combat-tested experience in the senior leaders who were forced out and have instilled a chilling effect on those who remain.

Hegseth has eroded military readiness by poor planning for the Iran war, requiring extended deployments; robbed the force of funding by failing to gain congressional support for a war supplemental spending bill; continued munitions shortfalls because he structured the budget to pay for them in expectation of a third partisan reconciliation bill; damaged retention in the force, as 53 percent of service members now want to leave earlier because of politicization; and caused allies to question the legality of U.S. military operations.

There will be a strong temptation among Hegseth’s adversaries to bring the military into the impeachment process by calling fired officers to testify as witnesses.

This would be a mistake, both normatively and practically. As a normative matter, it damages civil-military relations to place the military in the position of judging its civilian masters. What a democracy should want in febrile political moments is for the military to remain politically inert. Practically, what some envision as a long table of uniformed officers with glittering medals bearing witness to policy depredations would actually be a parade of suits explaining that they have no idea why they were relieved or forced into retirement.

The two fundamental tests of whether the U.S. model of civil-military relations is healthy are that the political leadership can fire any military officer and that the military will carry out the civilian leadership’s policies whether or not it agrees with the decisions. For all the destruction that Hegseth has visited upon the U.S. military, its professional adherence to subordination to civilian control remains strong.

That is yet one more reason the military deserves much better civilian leadership than Trump, the senators who confirmed Hegseth as defense secretary, and Hegseth himself have provided.

Kori Schake is a senior fellow and the director of foreign and defense policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute. She is the author of The State and the Soldier: A History of Civil-Military Relations in the United States. X: @KoriSchake

#5993. How America Can Counter Chinese Coercion

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

THEODORE BUNZEL is Managing Director and head of Lazard Geopolitical Advisory. He has worked in the political section of the U.S. Embassy in Moscow and at the U.S. Treasury Department.

EDWARD FISHMAN is Senior Fellow and Director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics at the Council on Foreign Relations. He is the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare.

ADDAR LEVI is Deputy General Counsel and Global Head of Regulatory Affairs at Lazard. She was previously the Acting General Counsel of the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

The Case for an Economic Security Alliance

Theodore Bunzel, Edward Fishman, and Addar Levi

Over the past year and a half, China has shown the world the power of its economic arsenal—starting with the United States. In April 2025, Beijing retaliated forcefully against U.S. tariffs, imposing matching across-the-board levies and export controls on rare-earth elements. This counterpunch rattled bond markets and disrupted auto supply chains, forcing Washington to seek a truce that persists to this day.

Next, China targeted Japan. After Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described a potential Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan as a “survival-threatening situation” that could justify deploying Japan’s Self-Defense Forces, in November 2025, Beijing imposed suffocating bans on rare-earth exports to the country. Reluctant to reinflame tensions with Beijing, Washington offered nothing more than token support. Tokyo has held firm, refusing to walk back Takaichi’s statement; the restrictions remain in force, and Japan’s mineral stockpiles are dwindling.

Then Europe came under fire. Fed up with a trade deficit with China that had reached $1.1 billion per day, the European Union began exploring new tariffs to counter Chinese overcapacity in May. As China threatened “resolute countermeasures,” French President Emmanuel Macron urged U.S. President Donald Trump at the G-7 summit in June to join forces in addressing global imbalances. But the United States elected to sit on the sidelines again, and Europe blinked, opting for talks with Beijing, with an October deadline set by Europe to take concrete steps toward reducing China’s trade surplus. The EU has since been in tense negotiations with Beijing over reducing exports of hybrid vehicles, chemicals, and machinery, taking on the threat of Chinese retaliation alone.

China, in other words, is exploiting the disunity between the United States and its partners. In a divide-and-conquer strategy that mirrors the Trump administration’s own globe-spanning tariff campaign, Beijing has broken the Western alliance into more manageable pieces, allowing it to fight actors one on one. Its market heft and control over critical minerals have been decisive, and as its fear of retaliation has diminished, it has rolled out more aggressive export restrictions and sanctions. In 2023 and 2024, Beijing added only five Western companies to its Unreliable Entity List, exposing them to financial and legal penalties; in 2025 alone, it added 76.

There is still hope for the United States and its allies—if they can relearn to act in concert. These countries should build a formal economic security alliance that establishes collective defense against economic coercion. The foundation of this alliance would be a pledge modeled on NATO’s Article 5, which considers an attack on one as an attack on all, in this case promising a joint response to economic coercion against any member of the alliance. Over time, this alliance could grow to address other economic challenges shared by members, just as NATO began as a security guarantee before evolving into a more integrated and expansive military alliance. It could adopt joint tariffs against Chinese overcapacity and currency manipulation, coordinate investment restrictions and export controls on advanced technology, and cooperate on critical minerals and AI development.

Amid transatlantic squabbles and European calls for “strategic autonomy,” a Western economic security alliance may seem more out of reach today than ever before. But enduring interests can outweigh temporary political friction. With the right policy shifts and trust-building measures—starting with the removal of Trump’s tariffs on allies and legislation that limits the U.S. president’s ability to reimpose them in the future—Washington can forge such a partnership and use it to check Chinese coercion.

The United States, Europe, and Japan are all confronting a major shared challenge: Beijing is intent on making the rest of the world more dependent on China and China less dependent on the rest of the world. Beijing subsidizes domestic production far beyond local demand, undervalues its currency by 20 to 30 percent, and enacts coercive economic measures—such as export controls and sanctions—to gain leverage over Western governments and companies and undermine policies it deems against its interest. The country’s resulting industrial overcapacity and surging exports, epitomized by a record $1.2 trillion trade surplus last year, threatens U.S., European, and Japanese industrial competitiveness and jobs. Beijing’s record of weaponizing its strengths also means that Chinese advancements in frontier technologies, such as artificial intelligence and connected vehicles, which continuously share data with external devices, pose security threats to Washington and all its partners.

Individually, the United States and its allies may struggle to match Beijing’s economic leverage, particularly its chokehold on rare-earth elements. But collectively, they are far stronger. The United States, Europe, and Japan alone produce around three times the amount of economic output that China does. They are home to the vast majority of the world’s most sophisticated companies. They also control critical inputs that China depends on, including lithography machines, specialized machinery for industrial production, chemicals, and aircraft engines. Despite efforts to reduce its dependence on the dollar, Beijing remains exposed to U.S. financial sanctions; only about 30 percent of China’s trade is settled in renminbi, and most of the rest is settled in dollars. The scholars Stephen Brooks and Ben Vagle have estimated that if the United States and its allies were to fully decouple from China, the harm to China’s GDP in the short run would be five to 11 times larger than that to U.S. GDP.

China is also more vulnerable than it appears. Despite an official GDP growth rate of five percent last year, the economic research firm Rhodium Group estimated that the country’s actual growth rate was 2.5 to 3.0 percent. China is undergoing a prolonged real estate crisis, state-driven overinvestment, and anemic domestic demand. With Beijing unwilling to address weak consumption, exports now fuel more than half of the country’s growth, according to Rhodium’s numbers, making access to Western markets China’s economic Achilles’ heel.

If history is any guide, these Western states should be able to coordinate to use their collective power. During the Cold War, they came together to form the Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls to restrict sales of military and dual-use technology to the Soviet Union. After the 1973 Arab oil embargo, Canada, Japan, the United States, and a large group of European countries established the International Energy Agency, which required members to share reserves with any member affected by a supply cut—effectively a mutual defense pact for energy. And during the 2008 financial crisis, the U.S. Federal Reserve and other allied central banks coordinated rate cuts and established emergency swap lines to avert another Great Depression.

Yet in recent years, collective economic initiatives among Western allies have been underwhelming. In 2021, the U.S.-EU Trade and Technology Council was created to coordinate industrial policy and export controls toward China, but it largely devolved into a talk shop. In 2023, the EU established its Anti-Coercion Instrument after China boycotted Lithuanian goods in response to the opening of a Taiwanese Representative Office in Vilnius, but it has yet to use it. That same year, the G-7 announced a new Coordination Platform on Economic Coercion, which pledged members to warn each other and cooperate against shared economic threats, such as China’s nonmarket policies and economic coercion on critical minerals. But the platform contained no binding commitments and has largely been ignored.

These initiatives foundered from a lack of urgency and a reluctance among European countries to antagonize China, which is one of their largest trading partners. They were also constrained by disputes between European countries and the Biden administration over steel and aluminum tariffs and the large domestic subsidies in the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act. But Trump’s second-term policies have been the nail in the coffin. U.S. tariffs and threats to annex Greenland have rattled trust among American allies. Washington’s trade truce with Beijing has dispelled illusions that the transatlantic partners form a united front and made European partners doubt that the United States will come to their aid. Calls are indeed growing within Europe for de-risking and “digital sovereignty”—but from the United States, not China.

These calls will not be easy to quiet, even if Trump is followed by a president focused less on tariffs and more on building alliances. During the Biden administration, allies told U.S. officials that they would not commit to larger-scale economic coordination on shared challenges regarding China, Ukraine, or the Middle East because they were concerned that a future U.S. president could erase the progress. Europe’s concerns are well founded. As American politics has become increasingly polarized, more power has amassed in the executive branch. Congress, which historically provided ballast in U.S. foreign policy, has been absent. When Trump announced sweeping duties under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act against U.S. allies in April 2025, Congress did effectively nothing. When the Supreme Court ruled these tariffs as unconstitutional, the administration pivoted to other tariff authorities, and again, Congress stood by. Rebuilding trust will therefore require an institutional remedy that goes beyond communiqués and professions that “America is back.”

There is reason to think that the United States can repair its ties. The country still has a strong economic relationship with Europe. The value of cross-border mergers and acquisitions and investments across the Atlantic last year remained mostly normal, and total trade in goods and services between the United States and the EU increased by nearly six percent over the course of 2025. There is also little evidence a major economic rupture is coming. Despite frustrations with Washington in European capitals, European businesses want to maintain ties with the United States.

More important, Europe has finally awoken to the economic threat from China, because the surge of auto and industrial exports from China to Europe poses an existential challenge for the continent’s economic model. Chinese auto exports to Europe increased by 29 percent in 2025 and by over 60 percent year-over-year in 2026 as European auto exports to China have flatlined. Germany’s mighty auto industry alone lost 50,000 jobs in 2025. Even Volkswagen, which lobbied against the EU’s tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024, has changed its tune. In July, its CEO all but urged the EU to extend tariffs to Chinese plug-in hybrids. Germany, which shed 74,000 industrial workers in non-auto sectors in 2025, has begun quietly identifying chokepoints it can use as leverage over China. Despite a provisional agreement with Beijing to curb Chinese hybrid vehicle exports in October, Brussels appears poised to unveil new measures against China on chemicals and machinery in the coming months as it finally grapples with the threat of Chinese industrial overcapacity.

These challenges will only get worse in the coming years and make Europe more likely to seek the United States’ help. And in Washington, the notion of a united Western front against Beijing has bipartisan resonance. As Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi have recently argued in Foreign Affairs, even if the Trump administration continues to alienate some European partners, shared interests will keep them open to allied cooperation when the next administration comes.

When it does, the most important step will be terminating every tariff—issued pursuant to Section 232, Section 301, Section 338, or Section 201—and pending investigation against any ally that was imposed during the second Trump administration. This would present both a unilateral demonstration of good faith and an opening gambit for negotiations on an economic security alliance. It would be a decisive break from Trump’s tariff policy and a rejection of Biden’s halfway model, which mostly turned tariffs into quotas and suspensions. It would be both politically popular, considering Americans’ dismal view of tariffs, and good for the economy, as the removal of duties could lower prices and accelerate growth. And because Trump’s tariffs have all been enacted via executive action, they can also be terminated that way.

As part of this first phase, the White House should also pledge support to any ally facing Chinese coercion, by providing targeted economic assistance or access to relevant stockpiles, such as the rare earths the Trump administration has begun amassing in its U.S. Strategic Critical Minerals Reserve. If the president made good on such pledges, it would demonstrate concrete benefits to potential members and build confidence in the alliance’s viability.

These unilateral measures would set the table for a formal economic security treaty. That treaty’s foundation would include an economic mutual defense commitment, mimicking NATO’s Article 5, which would go a long way toward restoring Western escalation dominance over China and therefore defanging Beijing’s threats. Such a pledge would have both defensive and offensive components. For defense, members would commit to providing targeted allies with economic assistance, preferential market access, and access to stockpiles of critical goods. Offensively, members would respond to coercion against an ally by applying joint sanctions, tariffs, or export controls. The United States, the EU, and Japan should form the core of this alliance given their individual economic and strategic heft, but other like-minded partners, such as Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom, should be welcome to join as well.

Ensuring the alliance’s longevity will require more than goodwill gestures carried out by executive action. The most durable approach would be a congressional-executive agreement backed by legislation, which would embed the alliance firmly in U.S. law and make it harder to unwind. Critically, this legislation should protect allies from the whims of future presidents. Over the years, Congress has delegated broad powers to the executive to impose tariffs for national security and other reasons—powers that recent administrations have used with reckless abandon. Congressional treaty legislation could codify the removal of these excessive tariffs and restrict any additional duties on alliance members unless approved by Congress. This self-limiting measure would give allies confidence that the bargain would survive changes of U.S. administrations. To address the possibility that novel legal theories could somehow be used by the executive branch in the future, the treaty legislation should also enact an automatic sunset after 60 days on any new duties on alliance members unless Congress affirmatively acts to retain them. Finally, the bill would pre-authorize rapid assistance to any ally facing foreign economic coercion, giving the executive the authority to honor the pact’s collective defense commitment.

These measures would be important not only to improve trust between governments but also between governments and the private sector. Firms make investment decisions based partly on whether they expect relations between countries to remain stable and predictable—often on a five- or ten-year time horizon, beyond any one U.S. presidential term. Today, in light of the transatlantic friction over trade and technology, many companies are debating whether to create separate operational and supply chain ecosystems for Europe and the United States. By constraining a future U.S. president’s ability to impose new tariffs on alliance members, an economic security pact would give companies confidence to build lasting economic links across the alliance system, even in the absence of a formal free-trade agreement.

Enacting ambitious legislation is always difficult, but there is reason to believe that U.S. lawmakers would be supportive of such an alliance. Chinese economic coercion is a bipartisan concern. Although some members of Congress may be wary of coming out against tariffs, the tool has become significantly less popular during Trump’s second term, and reclaiming congressional authority over tariff policy would serve Congress’s institutional interests. In a February survey by the Harris Poll, 72 percent of Americans agreed that Trump’s tariffs have had more of a negative than a positive impact, with 60 percent of Republicans agreeing that they have negatively impacted consumers. Tariffs on allies are especially unpopular: in an Ipsos poll conducted in August, Americans opposed placing additional tariffs on Canada by nearly three to one. Tariffs have also become closely associated with inflation. In an August poll conducted by the Council on Foreign Relations and Morning Consult, 75 percent of Americans reported being concerned about the price of food and groceries, and 83 percent of that group said that tariffs had increased those prices. With affordability now Americans’ number one concern, lawmakers have strong incentives to vote for legislation limiting tariffs.

The United States would have to lead the way for an economic security alliance, but just as important would be negotiations among potential members over the rules governing the pact itself. The agreement should spell out how collective defense would work in practice, specifying how allies can facilitate sharing commercial information and economic intelligence; who determines when economic coercion has occurred; and what kind of assistance, offensive and defensive, members can expect in such an event. If the alliance were successful in expanding its membership and scope, it could establish an independent secretariat to help it function, but the goal should be to make commitments credible without creating another sprawling international bureaucracy.

Collective economic defense would be just the starting point. Over time, the alliance could adapt to address a broader set of economic security challenges. On Chinese overcapacity, members could coordinate tariffs on the sectors most distorted by nonmarket practices such as subsidies and preferential financing, preventing Beijing from simply redirecting surplus exports from one allied market to another, or leverage a common baseline tariff on Chinese goods to compel Beijing to strengthen its undervalued currency. The same logic applies to export controls, which Western countries vary widely in applying. To break reliance on Chinese critical minerals, members could use the alliance to simplify the confusing set of international critical mineral initiatives underway by streamlining financing, making long-term purchase commitments, investing in processing, and building up stockpiles.

In this way, collective economic defense could follow a path similar to NATO. The North Atlantic alliance began with a relatively simple security guarantee that evolved into a cohesive military bloc: common institutions, shared planning, interoperable capabilities, and habits of cooperation that would have been difficult to create at the outset. An economic security alliance could evolve in much the same way. A credible promise of mutual defense would create the confidence needed for governments and firms to integrate more deeply over time.

To be sure, an economic zone for the free world would be an ambitious undertaking, especially at a moment of unusually low trust between the United States and its allies. But the United States, Europe, and Japan do not need to agree on all matters of economic statecraft to build such a space, nor do they need to trust that future governments will always share the same priorities. What they need are institutions that allow them to cooperate despite those disagreements and that make their most important commitments durable enough to survive political change.

Moments of geopolitical rupture have provided fertile ground for institution building in the past. NATO emerged amid doubts about whether U.S. support would continue after World War II. In 1956, the Suez crisis badly strained U.S.-British relations, but in the years following, Washington and London rebuilt their partnership and established the 1958 Mutual Defense Agreement, which solidified nuclear cooperation and further bound the two countries together. The economic turmoil of the early 1970s, including the United States’ controversial exit from the Bretton Woods system and the Arab oil embargo, ended up pushing the major industrial democracies toward regular economic coordination that evolved into the G-7. In each case, crisis created opportunity.

Today, the hardest part for Washington will be accepting constraints on its freedom to act unilaterally. Presidents of both parties have long been wary of legislative checks on executive power out of fear that binding their hands would signal weakness. But if American power is constrained by predictable rules, allies will be more comfortable depending on it. If allies fear American economic power, they will hedge against it. Washington, in reserving the right to turn its economic weapons against its allies, will struggle to mobilize the collective weight of its alliances in markets, technology, and capital.

China’s divide-and-conquer strategy has capitalized on distrust within the U.S. alliance system. Restoring that trust will require Washington to make commitments that persist no matter who occupies the White House. The central wager of an economic security alliance is that the United States can gain leverage over China by surrendering some leverage over its allies. An economic zone for the free world can turn the tide against China, but only if the United States ties itself to the mast.

#5992. Mamdani makes behind-the-scenes moves to shape 2028 Democratic presidential race

Asked about 2028, progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York brushes aside political speculation, says voters want Democrats in Congress focused on governing.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is quietly working towards a new goal: to become a progressive kingmaker in the burgeoning battle for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination.

The socialist mayor of the nation's most populous city, who can't run for president himself because he's not a natural-born U.S. citizen, has been meeting behind closed doors with labor leaders to highlight the need for a union-aligned or left-wing candidate to seek the presidency.

The mayor's moves come as he's reportedly said he's uncertain whether progressive champion Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, his close political ally, will run for the White House.

According to Axios, which was first to report the news, Mamdani is concerned that if Ocasio-Cortez stays out of the 2028 race, it could leave progressives without a standard-bearer to face off against a more centrist presidential frontrunner in the primary battle.

WILL TRUMP SIT OUT MAKING A 2028 ENDORSEMENT IN THE RACE TO SUCCEED HIM?

Then-New York City mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani holds hands with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at the end of a campaign rally in Queens on Oct. 26, 2025. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)

Mamdani, who is seen as a major powerbroker for the left wing of the Democratic Party after his historic 2025 mayoral election victory, argues that the progressive movement can't waste its momentum coming out of last week's trouncing of Republicans in the midterm elections, as Democrats won a massive House majority and control of the Senate.

A source familiar with Mamdani's 2028 conversations told Axios the mayor "wants the progressive ecosystem to mobilize quickly, strategically and efficiently if a moderate candidate is clearly on the rise,"

Meanwhile, Ocasio-Cortez is publicly pumping the brakes on speculation she'll launch a presidential campaign or bid for the Senate in New York, even as a newly formed group of activists is urging her run for the White House.

VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., departs following a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on July 22, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"I think the thing that's important here is the last thing that people want to hear from me or any other politician here is about the next election. And what they actually want to hear from us is about what we are going to do with the electoral results they just gave us on Tuesday," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters Monday night, pointing to the midterms.

The comments from Ocasio-Cortez, who was re-elected last week to a fifth term representing parts of New York City, came hours after the formal launch of Ready for AOC, a political group working to encourage her to run for president by showing her she has legions of supporters ready to mobilize on her behalf.

"A people-powered movement asking Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for President in 2028. No campaign. No money. Just names," is how the group described itself on social media.

But Ocasio-Cortez said voters are more concerned about congressional Democrats' immediate legislative agenda rather than speculating about the next election.

"I think people are less concerned about the horse race, and they want to know: What are the investigations we're going to be starting? What is the legislation that we're going to be starting?" she said.

Veteran Democratic strategist David Plouffe, campaign manager for former President Barack Obama's landmark 2008 White House victory and a senior advisor on then-Vice President Kamala Harris' 2024 bid, said last week, "If AOC runs, she's going to start, 20-25%, probably. The question is, can she add to that? If she doesn't run, then that is wide open. That's where I think someone like Abdul may say, 'Even though I just won, should I look at it?'"

Abdul El-Sayed celebrates his victory during an election night event with Michigan Democrats in Detroit, Nov. 4, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Plouffe, who was speaking at a forum hosted by Harvard University's Institute of Politics, was referring to Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who made history last week as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.

"That's the thing about this race. It's so wide open that there may be some people run who surprise us. I also think there'll be some people who don't run who'll surprise us," Plouffe added.

Ocasio-Cortez said in September that she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a White House run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker.

"I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a fundraising email to supporters.

The now-37-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a New York Times interview two months ago that her decision, which could happen sometime after the midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?"

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speak on Capitol Hill on Aug. 3, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Schumer, who turns 76 later this month, has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for sixth six-year term in the Senate.

Ocasio-Cortez isn't the only leading figure on the left who is mulling a presidential run. So is Rep. Ro Khanna of California, a top House progressive.

Allies of the soon-to-be six-term congressman last week launched a draft committee called "Run Ro" to build support and raise funds for a potential 2028 presidential campaign.

#5990. Massie moves to force Hegseth impeachment vote

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the issue could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie’s resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie’s resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

In an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

He predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie’s odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

The questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

“It’s going to be everybody’s conscience, and then they’ll have to live with that vote,” Massie said. “And they’re going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they’re not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?”

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: “I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he’ll he will see things differently.”

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

Last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The New Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Referring to Massie’s measure, Smith said, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”

“Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk,” Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie’s Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley said the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department’s uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth’s stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department’s civilians.

“By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized,” Kelley wrote.

Massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie’s measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution says, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:

The House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

#5989. Sotomayor lets loose on conservative Supreme Court with revealing wish: 'Crazy things'

As Republicans reel from their bruising midterm election losses, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor is hoping some of the court's biggest conservative rulings will eventually be overturned.

Speaking at a weekend civics education event at George Washington's Mount Vernon estate, the liberal justice singled out the court's landmark 2024 presidential immunity ruling, which shields presidents from criminal prosecution for actions taken within their core constitutional powers and provides presumptive protection for other official acts. Her colleagues, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, are both in their late 70s, raising questions about their potential retirements and whether a Democratic-controlled Senate could complicate Trump's efforts to replace them with fellow conservatives.

"We saw the outpouring of voters on Tuesday … I tell people all the time, there’s no excuse for not voting. There just isn’t. Apathy is not acceptable," Sotomayor said at

TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK'

United States Supreme Court Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor (L) and Associate Justice Clarence Thomas (R) pose for their official portrait at the East Conference Room of the Supreme Court building on October 7, 2022, in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"I dissent a lot. I’m hoping that the court will take back some of the crazy things that it’s done. I’m only joking — maybe not," she said at the same event. "No, seriously. Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor speaks with late-night host Stephen Colbert during "The Late Show" on Tuesday, September 9, 2025. (CBS/StephenColbert)

"There have been some systemic changes in my court’s jurisprudence in many areas of law," she stated. "We’ll settle down, too. Not quite sure when. But we will. And a new order will be established that people will begin to understand."

Sotomayor specifically singled out the Supreme Court's 2024 landmark ruling on presidential immunity as something she would like to see revisited.

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR ACCUSES BIDEN ADMINISTRATION OF 'COMPLETELY' CHICKENING OUT ON SUPREME COURT REFORM

(L-R) US Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts and US Supreme Court Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor look on prior to US President Joe Biden's State of the Union address in the House Chamber of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on March 7, 2024.  (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)

In Trump v. United States, the case in question, the court ruled that former presidents have absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions within their core constitutional powers and at least presumptive immunity for other official acts. The justices ruled that former presidents have no immunity from prosecution for unofficial conduct, leaving lower courts to distinguish between official acts protected by the decision and private conduct that remains subject to criminal prosecution.

Sotomayor sharply criticized the ruling in her 2024 dissent, arguing that the court's conservative majority had effectively turned the president into a "king above the law."

"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

“I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said ahead of Monday’s talks.

Last week, Iranian officials announced, via Qatari mediators, a two-day plan to build mutual trust. Day one would have the U.S. military lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and release some of Tehran’s frozen assets. In exchange, Iran would invite the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to its bombed nuclear sites. Day two would then see the Strait of Hormuz reopened, after which nuclear talks would resume.

There is a caveat, though: Washington must first agree to Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war, including canceling new U.S. sanctions on Iran and reinstating U.S. oil waivers.

Speaking on Sunday, Rubio characterized Iran’s conditions as “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

The U.S. president told CNN on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” that he will order the U.S. military to return to all-out war. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said.

Iranian state media accused the United States of firing “projectiles” at the strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Tehran also issued a warning to the United States that same day. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X, adding, “Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Such threats have made other Persian Gulf powers doubt the effectiveness of current peace talks. The region should “prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” senior Emirati official Anwar Gargash told Reuters on Monday.

Tuesday, Nov. 10: The United Arab Emirates hosts two-day trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visits Bulgaria.

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Spain’s largest unions hold a general strike.

Russia hosts a leaders’ meeting of the Collective Security Treaty Organization.

Thursday, Nov. 12: Danish lawmakers consider the joint defense agreement between Greenland and the United States.

Sunday, Nov. 15: The Philippines kicks off a three-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Cape Verde holds a presidential election.

Alleged China ties. Nvidia stocks plummeted as much as 8.8 percent during trading on Monday after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company’s board stressed over the weekend that there is “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Still, the U.S.-based corporation plans to open an immediate investigation into the incident. Jensen will continue to lead the company during the inquiry.

This past spring, Rubio drafted a classified memo warning top Trump administration officials that the Nvidia CEO was in a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang whom U.S. intelligence sources believe had been recruited to spy by China’s State Security Ministry. Alice Huang was the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, that the U.S. Commerce Department had investigated on suspicion that it was helping China smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted artificial intelligence chips. It is unclear if she is still employed at Megaspeed.

Jensen Huang is one of the world’s most consequential figures in the AI industry and an influential ally of Trump. Following news of Huang’s affair, Trump called Huang an “honorable guy” who has done “an amazing job for our country,” and he confirmed that he still plans to take Huang on his upcoming trip to China. On Monday, Beijing denied the espionage allegations.

Missing from COP31. This year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) kicked off in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday against a global backdrop of deadly flooding, surging fuel costs, and record-setting temperatures. The 12-day event is expected to prioritize curbing greenhouse gas emissions and advancing climate legislation.

“We want people to feel the results of climate ‌talks in ⁠daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford, and in new jobs,” Turkish COP31 President Murat Kurum said on Monday.

However, with the leaders of world’s top three carbon dioxide emitters—China, the United States, and India—not attending the event, experts expect that this year’s summit could amount to little. Other notable absences include Russian President Vladimir Putin, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. In fact, only a few of the 91 world leaders attending COP31 come from industrialized nations with significant carbon footprints.

Heading home? Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested new identity documents, including a passport, on Monday to enable her return from self-imposed exile in India, according to a letter seen by Reuters.

“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina told The Associated Press last week. Dhaka, however, has rejected her request, saying that it will not give a “passport to a terrorist.” Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for her deadly crackdown on student-led protests in the summer of 2024, during which as many as 1,400 people were killed, according to U.N. estimates.

Hasina “is a fugitive criminal,” said Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs. “We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over,” he added. New Delhi has yet to comment on Hasina’s request and Dhaka’s refusal. Previously, though, India has refused to surrender Hasina to Bangladeshi authorities, straining diplomatic ties between the neighboring nations.

On Sunday, a modern synagogue in Budapest transformed—for one night only—into a runway for Orthodox Jewish women hoping to challenge stereotypes about their modest dress code. Under that dress code, known as tzniut, Orthodox Jewish women are generally required to cover their collarbones, elbows, and knees; the rules also dictate that married women must cover their hair. Although some outsiders view these policies as restrictive, the organizers of the “Kosher & Chic” fashion show aimed to show that women can still dress to reflect their personalities while following modesty rules.

#5987. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

But as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

Saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

“Nobody could have predicted this,’’ said David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with new GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state’s sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state’s 14 House seats.

But the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown said, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you’ve taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, said redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

“Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren’t on anyone’s radar screen, so they didn’t think they had to do anything.”

Womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don’t make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you’re down on your luck and you don’t have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she said. “Most people don’t want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” said Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis said. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

“I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he said in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

“North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It’s been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he said.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn’t keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it’s a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”
