#5986. The Limits of China’s Self-Sufficiency

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

JOEL WUTHNOW is a Senior Research Fellow at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a co-author of China’s Quest for Military Supremacy. The views expressed here are his own.

Why the Country’s Food Insecurity Could Prevent a War Over Taiwan

When assessing the probability of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait, analysts tend to focus on a few obvious risks that China would face—namely, military defeat, economic slowdown, and restricted oil and technology imports. All of these are important, but an equally significant vulnerability is often left off the list: China’s reliance on soybean imports.

Beijing recognizes this liability. At the 20th Party Congress, in 2022, Chinese leader Xi Jinping identified “ensuring the security of food, energy resources, and critical industrial supply chains” as issues essential to national security and social stability. Food security, conspicuously listed first, is an especially sensitive issue for China’s 1.4 billion inhabitants: roughly 15 percent of the country’s population today was alive during the 1959–61 famine, which resulted in an estimated 30 million deaths.

As with technology and oil, Beijing has tried to limit its dependence on soybeans by building up stockpiles and diversifying its sources. But because soybeans are a fragile foodstuff, there is only so much China can do. Beijing can support a war effort, therefore, for only as long as the Chinese public could put the People’s Liberation Army’s success above its nutritional needs. And the key for deterring Chinese leaders from starting a conflict is to convince them that a domestic crisis would arrive sooner than any battlefield victory.

Disruption to critical imports is one of the most powerful deterrents to China’s use of force, and it’s a threat that the Chinese government has spent decades working to counter. The specter of a foreign blockade in the Strait of Malacca, through which most of Chinese oil imports pass, has worried Chinese leaders since at least 2003, when Chinese leader Hu Jintao warned about the risk of major powers’ interference creating a “Malacca dilemma” for China’s energy security. Beijing, however, has stockpiled massive reserves of oil, which it could complement in a crisis by increasing imports of Russian oil and, as Moscow has done, building up a sanctions-evading shadow fleet to transport oil from the Middle East.

Access to foreign technology is a newer but just as important concern, and China is similarly stockpiling critical components, such as chips. It is also having success in developing local alternatives. Beijing has already pulled ahead in some sectors, such as solar and battery manufacturing, or it is working to close the gap in others, as in semiconductors.

But Beijing has fewer options when it comes to self-sufficiency in food. Domestic production of staple grains—such as wheat, rice, and corn—accounts for more than 90 percent of consumption in these categories, but China remains dependent on foreign producers for other important foodstuffs, including soybeans, beef, and barley. Between 2000 and 2020, the share of China’s food supply provided by imports grew from six percent to 34 percent, and analysts predict it to increase to 41 percent by 2030. Part of this growth comes from the country’s economic development; as people become wealthier, their diets diversify, and they are no longer satisfied eating only grains. Between 1962 and 2024, meat as a percentage of the typical Chinese diet increased by a factor of 18.

This is where the central role of soybeans comes in. The legume provides a complex array of proteins in animal feed that other food sources and synthetic amino acids cannot replicate. Without it, livestock herds in China would shrink, thereby threatening domestic meat and dairy supplies. Soybean oil is also the most used cooking oil in China, making up nearly half the market. Alternatives, such as palm and rapeseed oils, are also mostly imported and face the same risks of maritime disruption, offering little relief.

China has invested a great deal in securing and, when possible, diversifying its access to foreign food sources. In 2013, a Chinese company bought Smithfield Foods, the United States’ largest pork producer. And state-owned enterprises such as COFCO International, a branch of China’s largest food and agriculture company, are buying farms and building logistical infrastructure in major agriculture-producing countries, such as Argentina and Brazil, which allows them to buy directly from farmers. Such direct investments provide a buffer against price volatility, giving Beijing more control over the volume and cost of supplies at their source. China has also steadily increased its own domestic meat production, which accounts for more than 90 percent of China’s demand. But such efforts do little to mitigate the effects of disruptions in maritime shipping—especially of soybeans, which is a supply chain that is fragile even in peacetime.

The central rub is that China has no choice but to import its soybeans. There is not enough arable land in China to both expand soybean cultivation and sustain self-reliance in staple grains. (Soybeans are also a much less efficient crop than corn or wheat in China’s arid north, making this tradeoff the economical choice.) But the countries that grow and export soybeans are almost all in the Western Hemisphere, which presents even more logistical challenges. When the trade war between the United States and China broke out in 2018, for instance, Beijing limited its U.S. soybean imports from 40 percent to about 20 percent of its supply, making up the difference with increased imports from Brazil. But Brazil’s poor infrastructure and frequent natural disasters make its harvest more susceptible to failure than the U.S. harvest. In 2024, one Brazilian state lost a quarter to a third of its soybean harvest because of flooding.

U.S. and Brazilian ports are also about as far from China as they could be. Brazil’s Santos port, for example, is more than 10,000 miles from Guangzhou, which takes 45 days to ship. Because of soybeans’ sensitivity to humidity, this distance means that ships often arrive in China with rotten cargo. For similar reasons, the legume is also difficult to stockpile. Unlike rice and wheat reserves, which Beijing claims could last for years, soybean reserves are smaller and must be replaced more frequently. Chinese stockpiles might be able to last only a few months if its imports were cut off. Although China has been experimenting with bioengineered supplements in an effort to reduce the amount of soybeans in animal feed, rising food demand is offsetting any gains. In other words, its dependence on soybean imports is only continuing to grow.

The outbreak of war between China and the United States would pose existential threats to this supply chain. In the most extreme scenario, the U.S. military could block shipments from the Western Hemisphere to China, which would take away most of the country’s soybean imports. China has no naval bases or forward forces in Latin America that could counter these efforts.

But China’s food supply chains would suffer from disruption even without a U.S. embargo or blockade. Any war in the Pacific would bring with it massive risk premiums for maritime shipment insurance that might cause shipping firms to balk. Such an effect has already been on display for shipping in the Red Sea, where Houthi missile threats have caused insurance costs to skyrocket since 2024. A war in the Pacific could be far more intense and costly because it would involve major navies, and ships could not route around the danger zone, making the long-haul journey from Brazil financially ruinous for many companies.

Beijing could, in theory, offer sovereign guarantees to offset firms’ insurance premiums. Even then, the firms transporting soybeans, most of which are owned by U.S. and allied country parties, might cease transporting products to China to avoid abetting a hostile regime, to steer clear of dangers that would put their employees at risk, and to head off possible future exposure to sanctions for doing business with the country.

Chinese analysts believe that China could circumvent some of these risks by using its own commercial fleet. Although this fleet has impressive capacity during peacetime—the Chinese shipping giant COSCO owns 468 dry bulk carriers—in wartime it would be stretched thin, facing demands to help move construction materials, industrial supplies, and foodstuffs for the People’s Liberation Army and to transport critical military materials such as coal and iron ore. Even available ships would likely lack personnel with the training needed to keep soybeans fresh during the long journey. And if ships tried to avoid the most dangerous sea-lanes, trips could take even longer, surpassing the 40 days that soybeans can be safely stored. Cargo might arrive rotten, if it arrived at all.

A war in the Pacific would not trigger an immediate food crisis in China. In the shorter term, the government could manage reduced imports by releasing supplies of soybeans, frozen pork, and other staples from state reserves. It could also reduce the minimum soybean inclusion rates for animal feed, which would slow livestock growth and cut meat output but which would be workable for a time. A few months of a managed crunch, however, is a best-case scenario. More likely is that panic buying and shipping disruptions would drain reserves faster than planned, turning a manageable shortfall into rising prices and visible shortages within months.

There is reason to believe, for instance, that Chinese stockpiles might not provide the short-term security they purport to. Over the last decade, local government warehouses meant to store emergency food supplies have been found empty or filled with rotten supplies, largely because of corruption. This not only calls into question how much extra food China truly has but also undermines public confidence in the government. In the case of a conflict, citizens conscious of the long-term disruption to come would begin panic buying and hoarding supplies. Whatever reserves do exist would eventually run out, with members of the elite likely being prioritized.

If the conflict dragged on, the situation would become increasingly dire. Agricultural producers, especially small farms, would be forced to cull their herds. Poultry, which requires especially high soybean content in its feed, would be the first casualty, which would then threaten the egg supply. Pork would be next. Cooking oils would grow scarce and expensive, making it difficult for restaurants and households to function. Eventually, public patience would wear thin: hoarding, protests over prices and shortages, and local officials diverting supplies could put mounting pressure on Beijing to end the war.

Unlike China’s vulnerabilities in energy or technology, the fragilities of the food system are endemic. If a conflict were to break out in the Pacific, the United States would not need to institute a blockade against China’s agricultural supplies or gather an international coalition to sanction China’s soybean imports. Soaring insurance costs and ship owners’ reluctance to sail into a war zone would be enough to squeeze the flow, and the Chinese government would have little recourse to stop it.

If Chinese leaders believed that they could achieve victory quickly and with few shots fired, they might take the bet. Deterrence, then, will require convincing them that they cannot. The United States, Taiwan, and other governments should invest in drones, rebuild munitions stockpiles, and ramp up messaging to China that a long, drawn-out conflict is likely. As long as China’s leaders believe that a war would be indecisive in its early stages, the threat of domestic crisis would be a powerful reason not to start one.

To Catch Up to China, America and Its Allies Must Dig

How the Search for Economic Security Will End in Geopolitical Calamity

Henry Farrell, Abraham Newman, and Yeling Tan

Demographic Decline, Political Paralysis, and the Fate of Great Powers

#5984. Dead felons, dog and now a prisoner: Spanberger voting rights letters draw fresh scrutiny

Fox News political analyst Gianno Caldwell slams Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger as the state rolls back policies for girls' sports. Caldwell also weighs in on antisemitism allegations against the New York Times.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's voting rights restoration effort is facing fresh scrutiny after a state letter indicating that voting rights had been restored was mailed in the name of a woman who remains incarcerated on a felony drug conviction.

Spanberger and Secretary of the Commonwealth Candi Mundon-King have faced criticism over a series of apparent errors, including a letter sent to a dog in Goochland County that died five years ago, another sent to a sheriff’s office in Hampton Roads addressed to "Betty No Last Name" and others mailed to the families of deceased felons.

A Virginia resident who requested anonymity contacted Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham, after receiving a voting rights restoration letter addressed to "Kayla Renae Vaughn," a source told Fox News Digital.

DEM AG'S ELECTION CRUSADE AGAINST TRUMP RUNS INTO EMBARRASSING DEAD-FELON BLUNDER BACK HOME

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, pictured, delivers remarks during an election night watch party for Virginia Democratic congressional candidate Elaine Luria, not pictured, at Holiday Inn Virginia Beach on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital obtained images of the letter from the Republican minority caucus in the Virginia House of Delegates. The document appears identical to other restoration letters previously reported, except for the recipient's name.

The resident has no known connection to Vaughn, according to the GOP caucus. Meanwhile, Vaughn remains in prison at the Central Virginia Correctional Unit in Chesterfield County, serving a 40-year sentence with 37 years suspended.

Vaughn was charged in Pearisburg in May 2023 with "Drugs: Manufacture/Distribute; Schedule I or II; Second Offense," according to state correctional records. She was sentenced in January 2025.

Fox News Digital sought comment from Vaughn and prison officials. The prison referred the inquiry to the Virginia Department of Corrections, which acknowledged receiving the request.

Virginia House Minority Leader Terry Kilgore, a Republican, demanded an explanation from Spanberger.

TROUBLING DISCOVERY ON STATE VOTER ROLLS SPARKS ACTION DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS: ‘SHOULD HAVE BEEN FIXED’

A letter to "Kayla Renae Vaughn" signed by Gov. Abigail Spanberger and Secretary Candi Mundon-King. (Office of Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham.)

A letter from Secretary Mundon-King and Gov. Spanberger to Kayla Vaughn (not pictured). (Office of Del. Tom Garrett, R-Buckingham)

"Restoring the rights of the dead is a failure. Restoring the rights of a dog is an embarrassment," Kilgore said, citing previous cases.

"Restoring the rights of someone still incarcerated on a felony conviction would represent a new level of carelessness. The Governor owes Virginia answers, and soon," Kilgore said.

Garrett did not respond to a request for comment but has previously criticized the administration's handling of voting rights restoration.

The letter signed by Spanberger and Mundon-King stated that the administration had a "completed review of the particulars of [Vaughn’s] case."

Garrett recently pointed to a lawsuit filed by former Virginia House Speaker Bill Howell, R-Stafford, challenging then-Gov. Terry McAuliffe's attempt to restore voting rights to felons through a "big, blanket order." The Virginia Supreme Court ruled that restoration decisions must be made individually, a precedent Garrett argues is relevant to the current controversy.

"[L]ook at the letters coming out of Governor Spanberger’s office. Every one of them claims the administration ‘reviewed the particulars of your individual case," Garrett said, citing the previous letter addressed to "Biscuit Rigsby," a dog in his district.

"They know the rule. They’re just betting no one notices the gap between what the letters say and what actually happened," said Garrett.

Spanberger and Mundon-King did not respond to requests for comment.

Spanberger has publicly described her restoration efforts as benefiting "people who had previously been convicted of a felony, had served their time, returned home, and simply wanted the dignity of being able to fully participate in our democracy," a description that does not apply to Vaughn, who remains incarcerated.

The voting rights amendment approved by Virginia voters on Nov. 3 also limits automatic restoration to people who have been "once released from incarceration."

The amendment provides for restoration without requiring individual action by the governor. It excludes people "serving a sentence of incarceration for a felony" and those who "do not understand the act of voting."

#5982. What to Know About Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Chinese Spy Scandal

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Explainer: What to Know About Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Chinese Spy Scandal

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

The affair has implications far beyond Huang and his family. As the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips used to power artificial intelligence models and data centers, Nvidia has become a critical node in U.S. national security; meanwhile, the global demand for its products has seen the company’s valuation balloon to more than $4 trillion. Export restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced chips—particularly to China—have become a cornerstone of U.S. technology policy, and Huang has developed a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump over the past two years.

The allegations first became public on Oct. 29, when the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence had concluded that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying on behalf of Beijing had developed a “close relationship” with the Nvidia chief executive.

The woman, Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), was an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence, she was recruited by China’s main intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, to gather information on Jensen Huang and help China gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, which have been restricted by U.S. export controls since 2022.

Megaspeed had previously been investigated by the U.S. Commerce Department on suspicion that it was helping to smuggle Nvidia’s AI chips into China, a claim that Megaspeed has denied. A statement from December 2025 posted on the company’s website says investigations by the U.S. government and Nvidia have produced “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities” and that it adheres to “all applicable export control regulations.”

It is not clear exactly what role Alice Huang currently plays at Megaspeed. The Singaporean company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Foreign Policy, but it said in a statement to the New York Times that it took the allegations around her actions “extremely seriously” and would “conduct a thorough internal investigation.”

Megaspeed’s website continues to list it as a key Nvidia partner, and Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in an interview last month that the relationship between the two companies was “normal and not unusual.”

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice Huang had pitched Chinese investors touting her ability to secure advanced Nvidia technology.

Tech billionaires spent big, and data centers became a lightning rod.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Trump’s latest proposal would cede the United States’ AI advantage.

China has consistently denied spying on Jensen Huang, with Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun slamming the allegations as “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China” in a briefing on Monday.

Trump—who was reportedly briefed on the intelligence on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang a year ago but did not act on it—is standing by the tech executive for the moment, telling reporters on Monday that Huang was a “very high-quality person” and an “amazing guy” who was “suffering greatly.” The U.S. president did not reveal when he first learned about the scandal, only saying it was “not too long ago.” Trump added that he had spoken to Huang earlier on Monday. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy, … and I really believe him,” Trump said.

Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the company’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment from Foreign Policy on the allegations against Huang.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced the launch of its own investigation on Sunday, which it said will be conducted by a “committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel.” “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” the announcement said. The company also said Huang would continue in his current role during the inquiry.

Huang said he would fully cooperate with the investigation. “I love our country and our company,” he wrote in his statement. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

But the market is already reacting. Nvidia stock dropped more than 5 percent on Monday and has plunged by more than 15 percent in the past week.

U.S. lawmakers also want answers. Republican Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—who chair the House committees on foreign affairs, the Chinese Communist Party, and intelligence, respectively—sent a letter to Huang and Nvidia last week requesting that he testify in front of their committees on Nov. 18, giving him a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

The scandal is likely to cast a shadow over Trump’s upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week—the third time this year that the two leaders will be meeting. Huang attended both of the previous meetings in Beijing and Washington as one of several U.S. tech CEOs whom Trump invited to join. Trump said he had no plans to bring up Huang’s case during next week’s trip but added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it.”

Trump’s embrace of Huang is likely to have its limits despite the public show of support thus far, said a former senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“I think it’s going to be much more difficult for [Trump] to embrace Jensen Huang politically or commercially in the midst of a major investigation that will be bipartisan on what happened, who knew, what was done about it,” said the official. “My guess is that the president may not say that he’s distanced himself, but I think Jensen will find that every time … he wants to meet with the president, it will be inconvenient on scheduling.”

Asked on Sunday whether Huang would join Trump on his trip to Shenzhen, the president said: “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

Update, Nov. 9, 2026: This article has been updated to add new remarks from U.S. President Donald Trump.

#5980. Liberal podcasters tell TPUSA to ‘f--- off’ as Charlie Kirk backlash costs them advertisers

Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, co-hosts of the 'I've Had It' podcast, address the backlash after apologizing for laughing at a joke about digging up Kirk’s body. (Credit: I've Had it Podcast - Nov. 8)

A source in the office of a prominent nationally elected Democrat called "I've Had It" podcast host Jennifer Welch a "sicko" after she allegedly sought help managing backlash over a joke about digging up Charlie Kirk's body. Welch denied the source's account as she and co-host Angie Sullivan renewed their attacks on Turning Point USA , with Sullivan telling the conservative organization to "f--- all the way off" despite the hosts' earlier apology.

The controversy has also cost the podcast advertisers. Cash App announced it was ending its sponsorship, saying on social media: "We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast." Luxury bedding company Boll and Branch also reportedly dropped its sponsorship, while Turning Point USA's Andrew Kolvet claimed on X that several other advertisers had withdrawn their support.

The hosts apologized over the weekend, but Sullivan subsequently told TPUSA to "f--- off" while Welch said her apology was motivated by her own convictions rather than pressure from the conservative organization.

"Alright there's a huge online, cancellation campaign from all the titty babies over at Turning Point who want the 'I've Had It' podcast canceled," Welch said in a video posted to the podcast's YouTube channel. She accused Turning Point USA of "spearheading" the campaign because they're "losers and they lost" and "want to prove to their donors we can cancel libs."

SOCIAL MEDIA HORRIFIED BY DAVE CHAPPELLE’S SICK ‘JOKE’ ABOUT CHARLIE KIRK’S MURDER

Co-hosts of the "I’ve Had It" podcast, Jennifer Welch and Angie "Pumps" Sullivan spoke on their show. ("I've Had It" YouTube channel)

"When we apologize for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn't for you. That was for us," Welch continued. "Because someone I loved very much died from gun violence two years ago, and I just didn't feel good about that. And that apology was so that when I advocate for commonsense gun reform that I'm doing it clean and clear. I don't expect you to understand this because at Turning Point y'all laugh at violence all the time."

FAR-LEFT PODCASTER CALLS FOR 'PISTOLS FIRING' TOWARD JD VANCE, DEFEATING HIM IN 2028

A Democratic source told Fox News Digital that Welch called them while seeking advice on how to manage the fallout from her comments. According to the source, Welch blamed Turning Point USA for the controversy rather than expressing remorse.

"I am not Turning Point. I'm a national Dem and we don't need people like her in this party because it is exactly what we don’t like about the hard right," the source said. The source also called Welch a "sicko" and estimated that the podcast had lost "tens of thousands" of dollars in sponsorships over the weekend. The source further alleged that Welch's team used ChatGPT to help formulate a response to the controversy and identify "ways out of this."

A supporter attends a vigil in memory of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, who was fatally shot during an event at Utah Valley University, outside the headquarters of Turning Point USA in Phoenix, Ariz., Sept.19, 2025.

Welch denied the claims in a text message to Fox News Digital, saying she had not spoken with a top Democrat and that the podcast had not used ChatGPT. "Those are both wholly untrue," she said.

A YEAR AFTER CHARLIE KIRK'S MURDER, SOME COMICS ARE CALLING OUT JOKES ABOUT HIS DEATH

"We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it, and we apologized," Welch said. She added that the podcast had removed the segment and donated to Everytown for Gun Safety, a gun-control advocacy organization.

"Turning Point, the group leading the cancellation against us, mocks violence and never apologizes," Welch added. "We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren’t going anywhere."

Jennifer Welch, co-host of the "I've Had It" podcast, was an Oklahoma City-based interior designer who starred in the short-lived Bravo reality show "Sweet Home Oklahoma" from 2017-2018. ("I've Had It" YouTube channel)

While discussing their apology, Welch called TPUSA a "hateful organization," and Sullivan said she was "not going to be lectured by these people."

"These people support representatives to Congress that protect pedophiles and sex traffickers. They're completely fine with American citizens being gunned down on the streets of Minnesota. They're fine with putting people in cages and treating them like animals," she continued. "And for those of you at Turning Point who are worried that I don't talk enough, but yet, you don't believe in universal human rights, I want you to hear me: F--- off. F--- all the way off."

TURNING POINT USA TURNS THE TABLES ON 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' AFTER LATE-NIGHT SKETCH MOCKS CAMPUS RECRUITERS

The controversy began during an episode last week in which Welch and Sullivan read social media posts celebrating Democratic victories in the midterm elections. Both laughed after Welch read one post saying, "We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." The hosts also suggested, without presenting evidence, that Kirk's accused killer supported President Donald Trump. Voter records, however, showed that he was unaffiliated and had not voted in the previous two general elections.

After the episode sparked backlash, Welch and Sullivan posted an apology Saturday saying they had laughed at an "insensitive joke" and "should not have laughed." They said there was "nothing funny about gun violence."

The hosts' remarks also drew criticism from Democrats, including strategist Kaivan Shroff. "They are not helping Democrats," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "They are hijacking the attention Democrats actually earned at the ballot box."

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

#5979. Senate Republicans lament midterms, weigh leadership election delay

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the new Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”

“I will vote for the delay,” he said. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

“If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he said, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the issues. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators said. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

John M. Donnelly contributed to the report.

#5978. America’s AI Ambitions Depend on Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

LIN CHIA-LUNG is Minister of Foreign Affairs of Taiwan.

Washington Cannot Achieve Tech Dominance on Its Own

The United States and China are locked in a global competition to determine who will dominate artificial intelligence and whether it will be democracies or autocracies that set the standards and values of the new digital age. The United States leads the world in the sophistication and power of its artificial intelligence models, and its innovation base and investment in research and development remain unparalleled.

But AI competition is much broader than modeling alone. It encompasses a technology ecosystem that includes power generation, servers, and deployment in real-world applications. Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has described the AI industry as a five-layer cake with energy at its base and chips, infrastructure, models, and applications above it. To win the AI race with China, the United States needs to maintain or establish an advantage in each of these layers. And to do that, the United States needs Taiwan.

Taiwan produces more than 90 percent of the world’s most cutting-edge semiconductors, making it indispensable to the United States’ AI industry. Taiwanese companies also assemble roughly 90 percent of the servers that power the global AI economy. With complementary strengths in manufacturing and design, respectively, Taiwan and the United States have built a mutually reinforcing partnership in AI that has underpinned U.S. leadership in the sector. Alongside democratic countries around the world that don’t want to rely on China for their technology needs, the U.S.-Taiwanese partnership has also made a secure AI supply chain possible.

Some policymakers in the United States have blamed Taiwan for the offshoring of U.S. semiconductor manufacturing. Although it is true that the United States no longer manufactures as large a share of the world’s chips as it did in the mid-twentieth century, this narrative obscures the larger story. Taiwan did not weaken the U.S. semiconductor industry. Instead, Taiwan has been crucial to maintaining the United States’ technological superiority. By carving out a niche in advanced manufacturing and supply chain management, Taiwan can help the United States maintain its advantage in innovation and R & D. As the stakes of the AI race grow, Taipei and Washington—and the rest of the democratic world—will need to work together to prevail.

First and foremost, AI relies on access to advanced semiconductors. For much of the 1950s through the 1970s, the United States dominated the entire chip industry, from design to manufacturing. As the Center for Strategic and International Studies notes, “The United States created the modern-day semiconductor industry and has historically led in the technology’s development.” But as chips became increasingly complex and expensive to produce, the industry became more specialized. Although Silicon Valley held on to its strong lead in chip design, it began to outsource manufacturing capacity to East Asia. Today, as Washington tries to revive manufacturing, understanding the sources of this shift are essential for determining how to most effectively rebuild U.S. capacity.

In fact, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry was born out of U.S.-Taiwanese cooperation. With the onset of globalization and expansion of free trade starting in the 1970s, U.S. companies accelerated their efforts to outsource chip manufacturing to overseas partners. Taiwan’s government, seeking to move up the global value chain, established the Industrial Technology Research Institute, an organization for nurturing new technology ventures and channeling R & D to industries; bought technology licenses from the United States; and built Hsinchu Science Park in northwestern Taiwan. Taiwan also invested heavily in education and training for engineers. As the semiconductor industry developed, large Taiwanese technology firms such as TSMC expanded their operations and countless small and medium-size enterprises contributed to supply chains, creating a virtuous cycle that encouraged entrepreneurship, strengthened regulations and standards, and promoted international cooperation.

The result was an industrial ecosystem that was specialized, collaborative, and difficult to replicate. This ecosystem freed up the United States to do what it does best: design incredibly complex chips. Taiwan’s investment in manufacturing not only lowered the cost of U.S. technology; it also meant that whatever Silicon Valley dreamed up, Taiwan was soon capable of building.

Taiwan’s success as a semiconductor powerhouse has therefore never been at the expense of the United States. Rather, it has been based on decades of collaboration, a division of labor, and mutual trust between Washington and Taipei. Today, the United States continues to lead the world in semiconductor innovation, design, and research and development, whereas Taiwan is at the forefront of advanced manufacturing, packaging, and supply chain integration. U.S. tech firms such as Nvidia, Apple, and Qualcomm need Taiwan’s manufacturing sector to turn their creative ideas into usable products. Rather than replace the United States, Taiwan enables American innovation to reach global markets.

Still, Taiwan understands Washington’s determination to strengthen domestic semiconductor production and is willing to support that effort. TSMC has committed to investing $265 billion in semiconductor fabrication plants in Arizona. More than 20 other Taiwanese companies have also invested billions of dollars in the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem, creating jobs and expanding manufacturing capacity in the United States.

For Taiwan, these investments strengthen the existing supply chain partnership with the United States. They will become even more important as the U.S. semiconductor ecosystem grows, because the United States will need to rely on Taiwan’s knowledge and network of suppliers and engineers, built up over decades, to sustainably develop its own industry. There is no contradiction between what’s good for the United States and what’s good for Taiwan: with demand for chips continuing to rise, both sides benefit from deeper partnership and the sharing of expertise and supply chain security.

The U.S.-Taiwanese partnership extends beyond chips. The United States boasts world-leading AI platforms and cloud service providers; Taiwan is the world’s leading manufacturer of the AI servers on which they run. Taiwanese companies such as Foxconn, which accounts for approximately 40 percent of the world’s AI server market, and Quanta Computer, which builds high-density AI servers and infrastructure for cloud service providers, manufacture the essential products and components underpinning the operations of major U.S. technology companies, including Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta.

The United States can expand its AI-related manufacturing capacity, but it would take many years for it to match the scale, supplier networks, engineering expertise, and manufacturing capabilities of Taiwan’s existing industry. It is far easier and cheaper for Taiwan to manufacture the infrastructure that enables U.S.-designed AI chips and platforms to be deployed rapidly and at scale. Even if the United States were to drastically expand its domestic manufacturing capacity, it would only be able to produce a fraction of what is needed to keep pace with AI demand.

The next phase of AI competition will be over how to apply the technology in the real world. The United States and China are going to be in a race to fuse AI with robots, drones, and other defense systems, as well as to integrate it into manufacturing, health care, and transportation. Indeed, this process is already well underway: robotic taxis, for instance, are now operating in cities such as San Francisco and Shenzhen, and companies in China and the United States are jockeying for leadership in the sector.

In the application of AI technology, Taiwan’s strengths also complement those of the United States. The island’s semiconductor, communications equipment, and precision machinery industries are precisely those that will be needed to build the physical systems that can use American AI models. Taiwanese companies such as Thunder Tiger are already developing AI-driven defense drones, demonstrating the growing potential for integrating artificial intelligence, precision engineering, and advanced electronics into civilian and military applications. As AI evolves from a purely digital technology to an essential component of factories, robots, and vehicles, Taiwan’s advanced hardware production base will be even more valuable to the United States.

As the AI race intensifies, it will also become a contest over values, data management, and trust. If the United States and its democratic allies and partners want to stay ahead in technology, they must work together to create secure and trustworthy AI ecosystems that reflect their principles.

Supply chain collaboration will be crucial because no single place can dominate every aspect of the AI ecosystem. The United States excels in innovation and is home to major platforms; Japan is a leader in specialized refining, recycling, and research into deep-sea resources, as well as in precision semiconductor manufacturing equipment; the Netherlands supplies advanced lithography machines needed to produce the most advanced chips; and Taiwan specializes in wafer fabrication and packaging. Only through coordination can these countries build efficient and secure AI supply chains while reducing their reliance on China for essential components.

International disruptions have reinforced the necessity of supply chain cooperation among democratic countries. The COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, exposed the weaknesses of the world’s global supply chain networks, a lesson reinforced by disruptions to trade flows in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and rising energy prices amid instability in the Middle East. In 2025, Taiwan proposed a global semiconductor democratic supply chain partnership initiative to jointly construct reliable systems that can withstand international disruptions. In this initiative, Taiwan seeks to harness cooperation among democratic countries to usher in a new era of growth in industries connected to high-end chips.

Taiwan and the United States have already made strides in technology cooperation. The U.S.-Taiwan Economic Prosperity Partnership Dialogue, a bilateral platform inaugurated in November 2020, has hosted high-level discussions on AI supply chain security, digital infrastructure, critical minerals, drone supply chains, and high-tech talent. These exchanges have helped U.S.-Taiwanese cooperation evolve beyond traditional trade and economic relations and paved the way for establishing a technological ecosystem that can bring together democratic partners and allies.

Taiwan also stands ready to ensure the safe and ethical usage of AI. Safety depends not only on the makeup of the AI model itself but also on the security and reliability of the hardware on which it operates—an area in which Taiwan can bring its expertise to bear. Taiwan and the United States can work together to increase cybersecurity, establish testing standards, and build reliable manufacturing systems to ensure that AI develops safely and can be trusted by the United States and its allies.

When it comes to the technology underpinning AI, Taiwan is not an adversary of the United States but its most trustworthy partner. In every layer of the AI “cake,” Taiwan and the United States have developed—and can continue to expand—a productive and mutually beneficial partnership. Taiwan is a force multiplier for the United States in artificial intelligence: it has the capability, reliability, and values necessary to support the United States’ technological ambitions. If Washington wants to compete effectively in AI, Taiwan is indispensable.

#5976. The Walls Close In on Hegseth

Analysis: The Walls Close In on Hegseth

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, who is among U.S. President Donald Trump’s biggest Republican critics on Capitol Hill, on Monday introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” In remarks on the House floor, Massie said that the defense secretary “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation.” He also said that Hegseth has demonstrated that he will remain a “threat” to the U.S. Constitution.

Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of waging the Iran war without congressional authorization and ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties. Other articles focus on lethal U.S. strikes on alleged drug boats near Latin America, which Massie described as “extrajudicial killings,” and the U.S. operation to capture former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The resolution characterized the Maduro raid as the unlawful “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader.”

Massie previously introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson blocked the effort—pushing it until after the midterms—by recessing the lower chamber early. The House now has until Wednesday to schedule a vote.

The chances of the articles passing are “far more likely now than before the election,” Massie told CNN on Monday. Impeaching Hegseth requires a simple majority vote in the House. However, Johnson urged lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth, stating that it would be a “terrible look” while the country is in the “middle of hostilities abroad.”

Meanwhile, top House Democrats are also lining up behind the effort to impeach Hegseth. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC News on Sunday that he’s a “hard yes” on the impeachment resolution and that he believes there will be “incredibly strong support” among the rest of House Democrats.

It’s harder to say whether there would be enough support in the GOP-controlled Senate to reach the two-thirds supermajority vote necessary to convict and remove Hegseth. It’s also an open question if there’s enough time in the current congressional session for there to be an impeachment trial in the Senate. But Democrats could also push to impeach Hegseth again in a new Congress.

Even if Hegseth survives impeachment and Trump continues to back him, the defense secretary is poised to face relentless scrutiny after Democrats assume control of Congress on Jan. 3. Democrats have made it clear that they plan to fully leverage their oversight powers—and that Hegseth will be in their crosshairs. This means investigations, hearings, and subpoenas are coming. Democrats have already indicated that they want more answers from Hegseth on everything from the Iran war to the boat strikes.

Rep. Adam Smith, the ranking member on the House Armed Services Committee, vowed to conduct “vigorous oversight” of the U.S. Defense Department in a new Congress. “The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people,” he said.

But as the walls close in around him, Hegseth has remained defiant.

In comments to reporters on Monday before Massie introduced the articles of impeachment, Hegseth made no apologies. “If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury, or Rough Rider, or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished,” he said. (Operation Epic Fury is the U.S. military’s name for the first phase of the Iran war, from February to May, while Operation Rough Rider is the Pentagon’s name for the U.S. military campaign against the Houthis in Yemen last spring.)

Last week, Hegseth released a video taking aim at his political opponents. “This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice,” he said.

The video landed poorly even among some Republicans. “@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” Sen. Thom Tillis posted on X. “This is about you,” he added, accusing Hegseth of displaying incompetence, offering bad advice to Trump, and being involved in “shameful” and embarrassing “episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis was seemingly referring to the Signalgate controversy—a major national security scandal that Hegseth was at the center of early last year.

In many ways, it comes as no surprise that Hegseth is now in the crosshairs of Democrats and Republicans alike. He’s been a combative and divisive Pentagon chief from the start, spending much of his energy waging culture wars—such as by moving to ban transgender people from serving in the military and targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion policies—while using the Defense Department as a platform to promote his far-right Christian views. He’s also ruffled feathers by pushing out top military leaders and denying promotions for Black and women soldiers. Meanwhile, Hegseth has had an extraordinarily contentious dynamic with the press, effectively hollowing out the Pentagon press corps after major outlets refused to agree to restrictions that he sought to impose on their reporting.

Hegseth has made a lot of enemies in Washington in the process, and he seems to have fewer allies by the day. Even months before the midterms, there were signs that some Republican lawmakers were souring on him. As Republicans play the blame game over their losses in the midterms, support for Hegseth appears to be cratering—even among GOP lawmakers who are wary of publicly supporting impeachment.

When asked about where he stands on impeaching Hegseth, Rep. James Comer, the chair of the House Oversight Committee, told NewsNation: “I can tell you with a high level of confidence that there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

On Monday, Rep. Don Bacon told reporters that he was weighing whether to support Massie’s impeachment resolution. But he also said that it would be better for Hegseth to resign. “I don’t think he was the right choice to begin with,” he said.

Trump has so far stood by Hegseth and pushed back against questions about the defense secretary’s job security. “He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said of Hegseth on Sunday. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say ‘let’s impeach’ somebody who did that.”

Hegseth has been among Trump’s most loyal cabinet secretaries since he returned to the White House, and critics have portrayed Hegseth as a prime example of the yes-men culture surrounding Trump. But loyalty hasn’t always paid off for those in the president’s orbit, as he has a history of turning on even his most faithful advisors. Recent reports suggest that Trump has been asking allies about a potential replacement for Hegseth. Trump has also acknowledged receiving calls from people who are unhappy with the Pentagon chief, though he said that he didn’t understand why.

#5975. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”
