#5930. Democrats accused of 'No Kings' hypocrisy over push to change voter-approved trans sports measures

The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses Democratic efforts to overturn voter-approved protections for girls’ sports, including measures in Washington and Colorado. They also examine divisions within the Republican Party as Reps. Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan compete for House leadership following the midterm elections.

Voters in two Democratic strongholds approved restrictions on transgender participation in girls' sports last week, delivering rare Republican victories amid a blue wave. But Democratic officials are already discussing ways to change the measures, drawing accusations of hypocrisy from Republicans who point to their support for the "No Kings" movement.

Colorado Gov.-elect Philip Weiser, who also criticized a separate ballot measure restricting gender-related surgeries for minors, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal , D-Wash., both raised objections to the measures approved in their respective states.

At his first post-election news conference, he suggested Colorado's Democratic-controlled legislature could revisit the voter-approved measures, saying that it is "statutory … and a natural and I believe appropriate role for the legislature to say ‘what are the adjustments that need to be added."

PRO-TRANS ACTIVISTS HOLD RALLY AGAINST WASHINGTON STATE BALLOT INITIATIVE TO PROTECT GIRLS SPORTS

Colorado voters approved ballot measures increasing penalties for fentanyl-related offenses, restricting transgender athletes from competing in sports designated for the opposite biological sex and prohibiting gender-related surgeries for minors. The measures passed even as Democrats swept into power across the state.

COLORADO MOM WHO SAID DAUGHTER WAS SECRETLY TRANSITIONED HELPS LEAD EFFORT TO BAN BOYS IN GIRLS' SPORTS

Colorado Gov.-elect Philip Weiser, pictured July 22, 2025, suggested changes to voter-approved ballot measures following the November 2026 election. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post via Getty Images)

Weiser did not respond to a request for comment.

Republicans in suburban Denver criticized the governor-elect, dubbing him "King Phil I" and characterizing his response as "know[ing] better than Colorado voters in a healthy democracy."

"But before the ink on the ballots is even dry, Governor-elect Phil Weiser is already signaling that the vote of the people is merely a ‘suggestion’. With Coloradans approving ballot measures to crack down on fentanyl and protect youth sports and children, Weiser walked up to the podium on Wednesday and essentially declared that the will of the majority needs to pass his personal vibe check first," the Adams County Republican Party said in a statement.

Republicans characterized Weiser’s position as "you voted for it, but I don’t like it…"

"No Kings," the Adams Republicans added, invoking the protest movement that Weiser has supported through participation in "No Kings" protests. The movement's demonstrations have criticized President Donald Trump over what organizers characterize as authoritarian conduct.

The Colorado House Republican caucus echoed the sentiment, adding in a statement: "If the Democrats truly believe there should be ‘No Kings’ in America, it is time they take their own advice."

'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS

Meanwhile, in Washington State, Jayapal condemned a similar measure approved by voters.

Initiative 638 prohibits students defined as "biologically male" from competing in girls' K-12 school sports and requires students seeking to participate on girls' teams to provide verification of their biological sex from a health care provider. The measure passed with approximately 56% support in the reliably Democratic state.

Following the election results, multiple local news outlets reported that Jayapal pledged to "take our state back" after voters approved the initiative.

"We're going to start planning for how we overturn these bad initiatives and how we go back to loving everyone with gender inclusivity the way we have for decades," she said, according to several reports.

Jayapal did not respond to a request for comment.

Critics also pointed to Jayapal's past support for "No Kings" protests, accusing her of contradicting her own rhetoric about respecting the will of voters.

One critic highlighted a November 2025 social media post in which Jayapal wrote: "We have democracy for a reason. America doesn’t belong to kings it belongs to the people and we're going to keep it that way."

Jayapal also faced previous criticism over her support for the "No Kings" movement after praising remarks by Britain's King Charles III during his visit to the United States.

Washington Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad signaled support for a legal challenge, calling the ballot measure "unconstitutional on its face" and indicating the party would "support [for] organizations planning to challenge it in court."

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., speaks during a House Budget Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on April 15, 2026. Jayapal criticized a Washington state ballot measure restricting transgender participation in girls' sports following the November election. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under Washington's Constitution, lawmakers cannot repeal a voter-approved initiative during its first two years but can amend it with a two-thirds vote in each legislative chamber. After two years, the legislature can amend or repeal the measure with a simple majority.

The controversy leaves Democrats in both states confronting a similar political dilemma: whether to preserve the restrictions voters approved or pursue changes through the legislative and judicial processes available to them.

#5928. Did China Play Jensen Huang?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

China Brief: Did China Play Jensen Huang?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

The highlights this week: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair with a Chinese spy, Chinese marriage registrations drop, and the United States and China extend their trade truce ahead of an expected meeting between their leaders.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s connections to Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Beijing, exploded into a major scandal this week. On Sunday, he admitted to having an extramarital affair, Nvidia stock dropped, and the company announced it was launching an investigation.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation, is a former executive at Megaspeed—a Singapore-based, China-linked cloud-computing company that is Nvidia’s largest chip customer in Southeast Asia. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in 2023, shortly after the United States under President Joe Biden imposed sweeping chip restrictions on China.

Megaspeed has been under scrutiny since 2024, when the U.S. Commerce Department opened a probe into whether it was diverting Nvidia chips to China. Yet late last year, Jensen Huang convinced U.S. President Donald Trump to allow exports of Nvidia’s advanced H200 chip to China, with the White House taking a 25 percent cut. Many of these chips seem to have been sold to Chinese shell companies.

All of this happened even though both Nvidia and the White House seemingly knew about the risks surrounding Alice Huang for months. Trump administration officials were reportedly warned about her connection to Jensen in a classified memo this spring but took no action. Nvidia, meanwhile, hired a public relations firm specializing in sex scandals last year.

So, how did this happen? It’s possible that Alice Huang is an agent for China’s Ministry of State Security and was tasked with honey trapping Jensen Huang. That would suggest Megaspeed, which has denied all allegations that it engaged in misconduct, was repurposed or even created as a vehicle for intelligence gathering and for illicitly obtaining U.S. chips.

But it’s equally plausible that the relationship came first. Alice Huang’s resume is hard to verify, but she seems to have worked in finance and tech for at least a decade. It wouldn’t be the first time that a billionaire businessman got involved with a younger woman who he convinced himself was a brilliant up-and-comer.

If that is the case, either Chinese intelligence became aware of the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang and pressured her to let them exploit it, or she took it to them herself.

As I have noted before, China’s intelligence apparatus is messy, with multiple competing groups inside the government. That leaves room for outsiders to act as intelligence entrepreneurs. Alice Huang may have been working both Jensen Huang and the Chinese government for her own business edge.

Other questions remain unanswered. One is whether Alice Huang persuaded Jensen Huang to do anything on behalf of the Chinese state that he wouldn’t have done anyway, since Nvidia has a vested interest in access to the Chinese market. That said, Nvidia’s intervention to help halt the Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed looks suspicious. (Megaspeed remains under investigation by the U.S. Justice Department.)

Of course, China also benefits from having a line into White House discussions, and we can’t know what Jensen Huang has told Trump about China behind closed doors. Trump’s China policy has certainly been soft, and he has blithely dismissed this week’s revelations.

But why did the Trump administration disregard the warning from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio about Huang’s connections to Chinese intelligence? And who leaked the story to the press, whether out of patriotic feeling or a desire to disadvantage a rival?

It’s certainly a convenient moment for U.S. politicians to distance themselves from the White House and an increasingly unpopular tech sector. A tougher stance on China may become a distinguishing mark for aspiring Republican leaders. Democrats are also seizing on the news as an example of the White House’s tolerance of corruption and foreign influence, and they will likely push for stronger chip restrictions in the new Congress.

Whatever the outcome of the Huang affair, the state of counterintelligence and cybersecurity under Trump remains dire, underscoring a need for root-and-branch reform.

Marriage registrations drop. China’s demographic crisis remains its biggest long-term problem, and the news keeps getting worse. New data shows marriage registrations falling to an 18-year low for the January-to-September period, with 4.65 million couples tying the knot, a nearly 10 percent drop.

For comparison, the United States sees around 2 million marriages in a full year with a population one-quarter the size of China’s. Childbearing is closely tied to marriage in China, so a low marriage rate also means a low birth rate. Children born outside of marriage and their single mothers still face legal and social obstacles, though their situation has improved in recent years.

Hong Kong dissident receives longer sentence. A Hong Kong court has sentenced Joshua Wong, the imprisoned young activist who became the face of the city’s democracy movement more than a decade ago, to another 10 years for supposed collusion with foreign powers. Wong was due for release in January.

Beijing has an interest in portraying Hong Kong’s democracy activists as tools of outside agents. Wong, however, is a cause célèbre among Western politicians—unlike other equally persecuted dissidents such as Macao’s Au Kam San. If the incoming U.S. Congress chooses to take up human rights issues again, Wong’s case will likely return to the spotlight.

U.S.-China trade truce extended. The U.S.-China trade truce was formally extended by another two months on Monday, running through Jan. 10, 2027. In theory, that leaves room for Chinese President Xi Jinping and Trump to ink a more permanent deal if they meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week.

Xi is well aware of Trump’s need for some kind of victory, and as a result the Chinese leader is likely to come out ahead in any agreement. Whatever deal they reach may not last long: Domestic political pressure in the United States could blow it up before it is in place, especially in the wake of the Huang case.

Japan squabble deepens. Beijing’s relations with Tokyo remain frozen nearly a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Japan might be obliged to come to Taiwan’s aid if China invaded the self-ruled island. Even at the provincial level, Chinese officials are competing to look tough on Japan.

That is a perennial popularity-booster with both the Chinese Communist Party and the public, for whom the trauma of Japan’s brutal invasion lingers eight decades on.

Now, flights between the two countries are being slashed. Airlines, mostly Chinese, have scheduled nearly 700,000 fewer seats on China-Japan flights this winter, a drop of around 20 percent compared to last year. Takaichi’s stance remains popular at home, and she may be emboldened if a tougher U.S. policy toward China emerges next year.

James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social

#5927. A Recipe for Disaster in Taiwan

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

REBECCA LISSNER is Senior Fellow for U.S. Foreign Policy and Director of the Future of American Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations. She served as Deputy Assistant to the President and Principal Deputy National Security Adviser to the Vice President during the Biden administration.

MIRA RAPP-HOOPER is a Visiting Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. She was Special Assistant to the President and Senior Director for East Asia and Oceania and Director for Indo-Pacific Strategy at the U.S. National Security Council during the Biden administration.

Just a few years ago, U.S. President Joe Biden caused a stir when he confirmed publicly that his administration would defend Taiwan if the island were attacked by China—a divergence from the traditional U.S. policy of strategic ambiguity, in which Washington does not commit to taking any particular action. In May, U.S. President Donald Trump made waves for taking a different position. In a television interview, he described Taiwan as “a very good negotiating chip” in dealings with Beijing and mused that the island was close to China but far from the United States, implying that U.S. interests in Taiwan were negligible. In doing so, Trump seemed to confirm something many Asia watchers had feared: that this U.S. president would be willing to loosen the United States’ commitment to Taiwan to bolster his relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

A few days later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that there had been no change in U.S. policy toward Taiwan. But Trump’s words were alarming nonetheless—in part because they reflect a shift in Washington that goes beyond the Oval Office. Since 2025, politicians from both parties have been shying away from affirming the United States’ long-standing support for Taiwan. Meanwhile, China is developing new strategies to coerce Taiwan without going to war, and Beijing will be increasingly tempted to use them if it judges that the U.S. commitment to Taiwan is waning among both politicians and the public.

Yet that would be a grave miscalculation on China’s part. In fact, the United States’ interests in Taiwan are growing, not diminishing. Whatever the nature of Washington’s rhetoric right now, the United States would have to respond to any action by Beijing that threatened those interests, and both countries would then face a great-power crisis. To defuse this dangerous situation, American leaders must update the United States’ Taiwan strategy to reflect a new reality—and they should begin immediately.

Taiwan’s unique international status has long made U.S. policy complex. The Republic of China, now known as Taiwan, was a World War II ally of the United States. When the People’s Republic of China was founded on the mainland, in 1949, the Republic of China’s president, Chiang Kai-shek, decamped to Taiwan, and the United States maintained formal diplomatic ties with Chiang’s government, not the People’s Republic of China. In 1954, as the Cold War crested in the Pacific, the United States concluded a formal mutual defense treaty with Taiwan, in part to forestall increasingly aggressive artillery barrages from the mainland. Nearly 20 years later, however, when U.S. President Richard Nixon and his national security adviser, Henry Kissinger, began to engineer a diplomatic opening to the government in Beijing, they knew it would cost Taiwan.

In part because they understood that building diplomatic ties with Beijing would be painful for Taiwan and cause controversy in Congress, where Taipei had many boosters, Nixon and Kissinger slow-walked the process. So did Nixon’s successor, President Gerald Ford. It finally fell to President Jimmy Carter to make the change. On January 1, 1979, the United States ended its alliance with Taiwan and recognized the mainland government as “the sole legal Government of China.” Congress was irate. Lawmakers from both parties quickly drafted the 1979 Taiwan Relations Act, which remains in force. The law requires Washington to provide Taipei with defensive arms, creating the trappings of an alliance with Taiwan despite the relationship’s unofficial status. In 1982, the Reagan administration made an additional set of commitments to Taiwan, known as the Six Assurances. These include an affirmation that Washington does not endorse Beijing’s sovereignty claims over Taiwan and a promise that the United States would not use arms sales to Taiwan as a bargaining chip.

In the 50 years since, U.S. Taiwan policy has been remarkably successful. Through its partnership and arms sales, the United States has helped underwrite peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait, and Taiwan has thrived as a democracy and an economy, even as Washington has maintained a relationship with Beijing. But U.S. commitments to Taiwan have lately come under increasing strain. China has proceeded with a massive military buildup designed to give Beijing the option to take Taiwan by force; used coercive economic tactics, launched cyberattacks, and interfered in elections to put pressure on Taipei; and run frequent army and coast guard exercises to demonstrate its ability to strangle the island. All of this has stoked concerns across the Pacific that the United States’ long-standing partnership might not be enough to keep the peace in the Taiwan Strait.

The fear that China could attempt to retake Taiwan by force, possibly during Xi’s tenure, has grown in recent years. Analysts have frequently cited 2027 as the beginning of the window of maximum danger, based on a 2021 statement made by Philip Davidson, the former commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, about when the People’s Liberation Army might be prepared for an invasion. But this timeline was never hard and fast, and Xi’s recent purge of more than 100 officers has likely delayed the military’s readiness. U.S. intelligence assessments do not anticipate an invasion of Taiwan next year, and most scholars believe the Chinese government would consider such a move as a last resort only if unification could not be accomplished by other means.

The primary danger now is that Xi will escalate a pressure campaign designed to coerce Taiwan into negotiating a change in its status. Since 2025, China’s leaders have used their diplomatic channels to the Trump administration, including Xi’s direct line to Trump, to insist on American concessions on Taiwan in exchange for progress in trade talks. In May, China secured a pause on a planned $14 billion U.S. arms sale and other defense funding for Taiwan. Beijing may hope that additional incremental moves will further weaken Taiwanese confidence in the United States and that such actions will be difficult for Trump or a future U.S. president to reverse.

China is also clearly planning for more dramatic forms of coercion. It has a few options: since 2022, China’s military has practiced blockades of Taiwan, and its coast guard has simulated a quarantine of the island’s major ports. Beijing could also use customs enforcement or other administrative measures to attempt to assert its jurisdiction over Taiwan while minimizing the likelihood that the United States would intervene to stop it. If Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, who favors Taiwanese independence but has not pursued it in office, is reelected in 2028 and Chinese leaders believe that the path to a peaceful unification is closing, Xi may consider using these tools against the island in late 2028 or early 2029, before a new U.S. administration takes office. Given Trump’s alienation of U.S. allies in Asia and Europe and Washington’s limited means to respond to a maritime quarantine, Beijing might hope to get away with such a large-scale coercion campaign without inviting serious pushback.

Taiwan’s growing strategic importance makes Beijing’s development of new coercive options more concerning. Washington is no longer maintaining a partnership with Taipei because of a historical commitment or, as Beijing would have the world believe, to needle China. The artificial intelligence boom has put Taiwan at the center of the global economy. Taiwan is a critical supplier for the U.S. tech industry, and the United States recognizes that it cannot be a leader in AI without Taiwan.

The scale of the United States’ economic dependence on Taiwan is revealing. Taiwan is the country’s fifth-largest trading partner; a Chinese blockade of the island would imperil more than $250 billion in trade and could shave more than three percent off U.S. GDP in a year, according to a Bloomberg report. As much as 97 percent of the global supply of the high-end logic chips used in smartphones and other advanced electronics are produced or packaged in Taiwan. Losing access to Taiwanese chips could reduce advanced electronics production globally by 60 percent, with factories forced to rely on their chip inventories. The United States’ auto and medical device industries could deplete their inventories in a matter of weeks. The U.S. firms Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia are among the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s ten largest customers, which together represent more than $14 trillion in market capitalization. With AI growth buoying the U.S. stock market and the broader economy, a crisis in Taiwan would trigger a crash—potentially one similar in scale to the stock market crash at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The economic effects of a Chinese effort to squeeze Taiwan would not be limited to the United States. The research firm Rhodium Group has conservatively estimated that a yearlong blockade of the island could cost the global economy between $2 trillion and $3 trillion. A full-scale war would be far worse; Bloomberg has estimated that it would cause $10 trillion in economic losses and a global recession. It is therefore increasingly likely that the United States would be forced to act if Taiwan’s supply chains were put in jeopardy. The cost of standing aside would simply be too high.

Yet just when the United States needs to be doing all it can to prevent a crisis, Washington’s support for Taiwan appears to be wobbling. Trump’s musings about Taiwan’s geographical distance from the United States and his use of arms sales as a bargaining chip are the headline examples, but they are not the only indicators of a shaky U.S. commitment. Policy analysts have argued that the United States should change its position to definitively oppose Taiwanese independence or even withdraw U.S. forces from the military bases in Japan and the Philippines that are closest to Taiwan.

Public opinion in the United States is shifting, too. Americans’ feelings toward China have warmed considerably over the past two years, according to a July 2026 Chicago Council on Global Affairs survey. A majority, 57 percent, support friendly cooperation and engagement with China, whereas 40 percent support an active effort to limit the growth of China’s power. The share of Americans who see China’s territorial ambitions as “a critical threat” has decreased by more than ten percentage points since 2022, and those who favor the use of U.S. troops if China invaded Taiwan has fallen from 52 percent to just 38 percent.

In part, the declining support for defending Taiwan reflects Americans’ growing wariness of instability and conflict. A sense that the world was descending into chaos helped fuel Trump’s 2024 campaign; as president, Trump has heightened that sense by taking assertive military action in places such as Iran and Venezuela. Americans are now suffering the economic consequences of nine months of war in the Middle East, further deepening antiwar sentiment, as the midterm election results vividly demonstrate. Candidates for office used to clamor to sound tough on China, but many now blanch at the idea of suggesting that the U.S. military should defend Taiwan against a Chinese invasion, calculating that this is not the time to be seen as a hawk.

Of course, public attitudes can change quickly during a crisis. If China actually committed aggression against Taiwan, Americans could become more supportive of a strong U.S. response. And if the early stages of a conflict saw American casualties or a Chinese attack on U.S. critical infrastructure, the U.S. public could very well rally around the flag and demand a muscular intervention.

For now, however, China may believe that the United States’ will and ability to fight are both diminishing. The war with Iran has substantially reduced U.S. military readiness for a Taiwan contingency. The United States has used up much of its missile defense stock, including roughly two-thirds of its Patriot interceptor inventory, which was already depleted by U.S. aid to Ukraine, and as much as 80 percent of THAAD interceptors against Iranian drones and missiles. Even before the Iran war, analysts had warned that the U.S. military could run out of long-range, precision-guided munitions in a fight over Taiwan; now, the munitions shortfalls have become perilously acute. The war has also drawn military assets away from the Indo-Pacific. In August, Washington moved its last aircraft carrier in Asia, the USS George Washington, out of the region. It has also relocated missile defense systems to the Middle East, including Patriot and THAAD systems that had been deployed in South Korea.

The result is an increased risk of dangerous miscalculation. Should Chinese leaders assess that the United States’ commitment to Taiwan is wavering in both political parties and that the country is ill prepared for a fight, they might conclude that they have an opportunity to pressure Taiwan without inviting an American response. Yet because the United States has a greater interest in Taiwan today than at any point in history, Beijing’s bet could turn out to be wrong. China could announce a maritime quarantine of Taiwan or another coercive measure only to have the United States intervene, potentially prompting a great-power standoff.

Avoiding such a showdown will require American leaders to recommit to deterrence. First, Washington needs to update the way it communicates its positions. In their public remarks, policymakers should clearly state that the U.S. economy’s dependence on Taiwanese exports makes peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait a vital interest of the United States. American political leaders should emphasize to Beijing that the United States has an obligation to prevent a crisis that would tank the U.S. stock market, cut critical supply chains, and fell many American industries.

Clarifying U.S. interests would not impugn 50 years of careful diplomacy with China, nor would it require any change to U.S. policy as established by the Taiwan Relations Act, the Six Assurances, or the series of joint U.S.-Chinese statements, made between 1972 and 1982, known as the Three Communiqués. The updated statements, rather, would convey to Chinese leaders that certain changes to the cross-strait status quo would be unacceptable to the United States, even if Taiwan were to acquiesce to those changes under pressure. Washington would support a peaceful unification, for example, only if the process guaranteed the security of critical supply chains.

Once the United States makes its interests clear, it will also have to back up its statements with a new playbook to deter Chinese actions that fall below the military threshold. Beijing may already be in the early stages of imposing a quarantine on the island. Washington should not tolerate additional measures that interfere with commerce and maritime traffic in and out of Taiwan. To deter China from taking such steps, the next U.S. Congress should use legislation to clarify its wholesale, bipartisan opposition to Chinese blockades, quarantines, and other restrictions. Even if the White House continued to take a softer position, this would send a message to Beijing that other political actors might force the president’s hand. Congress should also press the administration to prepare punitive diplomatic and financial measures for use in the event of an escalating Chinese quarantine of Taiwan. By planning these reprisals well ahead of any coercive action, Washington would signal that a maritime pressure campaign would entail clear costs for Beijing and carry dangerous escalation risks.

The United States should strengthen military deterrence, too. The next Congress must pressure the Trump administration to release the stalled $14 billion package of arms sales to Taiwan, as well as other security assistance the administration is slow-rolling. Congress has a legal obligation to do so under the Taiwan Relations Act. Pausing security aid violates U.S. policy, and allowing the Trump team to make this concession in its likely quixotic pursuit of rapprochement with Xi only weakens Washington’s hand.

Washington does not have to—and shouldn’t—take these steps alone. U.S. allies such as Germany, Japan, and South Korea would suffer nearly as much as the United States if China were to take control of Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. These countries have an interest in working quietly together to deter and develop joint responses to Chinese coercion while also collaborating to diversify their chip supply chains and make them more resilient. In the United States, this work does not have to wait for a new presidential administration. Congress can send delegations and use other diplomatic opportunities to start developing plans with parliamentary counterparts abroad.

As the 2028 U.S. presidential election approaches, moreover, candidates from both parties should speak clearly about the country’s strong economic interests in Taiwan and about their commitment to deterrence. This does not require embracing bellicose positions, but presidential candidates do need to state firmly that any move by Beijing to choke off vital supply chains would harm U.S. interests and demand an American response. Consistent messaging would also signal to China’s leaders that they should not expect a future administration to be bound by Trump’s policy concessions—and signal to allies that come 2029, the United States will again be a reliable partner in standing up to China’s economic aggression.

The United States needs to update its Taiwan policy, but ceding ground as Trump has done only makes the cross-strait balance less stable. Unlike other Cold War–era policies, the importance of preventing Chinese aggression against Taiwan has become more—not less—vital with the passage of time. U.S. interests in Taiwan are plainer and easier to explain than they have ever been. Only by stating those interests clearly and backing up the words with actions can the United States continue to avert a crisis or conflict that would be devastating for all.

#5926. Senate GOP rebellion fizzles as Thune keeps power despite historic midterm massacre

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., isn’t ready to back John Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader. He and other Republicans want specifics on how Thune, or another contender, would get work done as Democrats prepare to take control.

There was neither an exodus nor a mass housecleaning in the Senate GOP leadership, despite frustration and rumblings of discontent among some lawmakers reeling from last week’s devastating midterm losses.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., secured another term as the top Republican behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, where lawmakers charted their course for their few remaining weeks in power and beyond.

Thune, along with the bulk of his leadership team, which now includes Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, were swiftly elected after a group of Republicans failed to delay the leadership elections.

It wasn't without a fight, though, with conversations behind closed doors dragging on for over seven hours.

GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., talks with reporters in the Capitol Visitor Center on Nov. 9, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., led the charge to delay, and didn't stick around after his attempts to do so failed on a 31 to 15 vote in the Old Senate Chamber to proceed with the scheduled election.

Johnson and others wanted to have a deep conversation about what had happened during the midterm elections, and a roadmap on what Republican leadership candidates could accomplish with the little time they had left in power.

SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER

But there was no opposition to any of the lawmakers running for leadership.

"This has never been anything against John Thune," Johnson said. "I think he has been very unfairly attacked, you know, by our base, and I don't agree with that. What I didn't agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position."

On Monday, Thune was adamant that he’d still run but was unsure of the outcome.

"That's the hope," Thune said when asked if he had the Senate GOP’s support. "You never know right until they vote."

Before the vote, Johnson and a handful of others believed there should be a shakeup in leadership, but didn’t offer an alternative to Thune.

"After the stunning defeat, you just can't continue on business as usual," Johnson said. "I mean, that kind of defeat demands change."

When asked if he’d be interested in running, Johnson said, "That’s part of the problem. Would you want it?"

"I think there's a number of people with talent," Johnson said. "Again, I'm not — at a minimum, we need to see out of our leadership team what's the strategy moving forward, and you can't come off of a defeat like that and just ram through elections and oh yeah, ‘let's just elect that leadership team by acclamation.’"

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., had previously run for leader twice and most recently against Thune. But the lawmaker, who joined Johnson’s crusade for change, declined to throw his hat into the arena again.

"I think we have to acknowledge the voters are not happy," Scott said. "We have to start listening to voters."

CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—'

Sen. Ron Johnson speaks during a hearing of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Feb. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Scott wanted ironclad promises on the GOP’s to-do list, including ramming through judicial nominees, government funding "without a massive omnibus," a stock trade ban, permitting reform, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, taking another crack at the SAVE America Act and balancing the budget — possibly through budget reconciliation.

Johnson and Scott were joined by Sens. Ted Budd, R-N.C., Mike Lee, R-Utah, John Kennedy, R-La., Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., in a push to delay the elections that was not met, and the would-be coup faded as the secret ballots were cast.

Still, there were others outside that cohort who weren’t happy with last week and believed that there should be deeper soul-searching on what Republicans did over the last two years that led to a historic night for Senate Democrats.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., contended that much of what the GOP listed as accomplishments over their time in power is what worked against them.

"And, you know, you have the kind of record that this Congress has had, I think we better have a pretty tough family conversation about what it is we're doing," Hawley said.

"When you cut Medicaid, but you fund data centers, when you cut rural hospital funding, but you fund Planned Parenthood, when you let the cost of healthcare for working people go through the roof, but you can't do anything for them on other issues of affordability, from fertilizer to gas," he continued. "Yeah you know what? The public doesn’t like that very much."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#5924. The New Epicenter of Global Terror

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

EGHOSA E. OSAGHAE is Director-General of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs.

How Africa’s Weak States and Rare Earths Drive Transnational Extremism

Twenty-five years after 9/11, much of the world has moved on from the war on terrorism. Following the defeat of the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria and the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, Washington has turned to other major concerns; along with many of its European allies, the United States has been more preoccupied with the growing confrontation with China, and with the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, than with the threat of transnational extremism. Buttressing this shift has been a general decline in terrorist attacks in many parts of the world since ISIS’s peak, in the mid-2010s.

Yet there is one region of the world where terrorism not only persists but also appears to be growing. According to reports by the United Nations and the Global Terrorism Index, Africa is the overwhelming center of terrorist activity today. The African continent accounts for more than 50 percent of all global terrorism-related deaths over the past five years. It also hosts three of the four deadliest jihadi groups in the world: ISIS, which is now primarily based in Africa, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), and al-Shabab. (The fourth is Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, also known as the Pakistani Taliban.) Six of the ten countries that are most affected by terrorism are also in Africa: Burkina Faso, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, and Somalia. And whereas the Middle East has had a 93 percent decline in terrorist attacks between 2017 and 2025, the Sahel has experienced a 17 percent growth over the same period, with a record 4,043 terrorism deaths in 2023 alone.

To the extent that African terrorism has attracted global concern, much of the attention has focused on the Sahel region. The broad swath of land separating the Sahara and the Maghreb in the north from sub-Saharan Africa is a hotbed of extremism, hosting JNIM and ISIS affiliates such as Boko Haram in Nigeria, Cameroon, and Chad, as well as bandit groups such as Lakurawa in Niger and Nigeria and al-Shabab in Somalia. But terrorist activity in Africa now extends to a host of other countries in western, central, and southern Africa as well, including Benin, the Central African Republic, Mozambique, and Togo. Many of these countries have little previous history of jihadi ideology or extremist violence.

World leaders overlook this continent-wide terrorist threat at their own peril. Not only have terrorist groups become a major challenge to African stability and development; they also pose a growing danger to global security. For now, these groups may appear to have little capacity to project their power beyond Africa’s borders. Yet amid the new scramble for Africa’s mineral resources—and for influence on the continent—this may change. Global powers, especially China and Russia, have been increasing their efforts to gain economic, political, and military leverage in Africa, which has in turn undermined collective international initiatives to fight terrorism. And many African jihadi groups themselves have strong anti-Western sentiments and have been using the resource wars to help build transnational networks.

Thus far, the global response to the African threat has largely focused on military operations, especially in the Sahel. But to truly address the phenomenon, outside powers and world leaders will need to understand the underlying forces that have led to this proliferation of extremist groups. Above all, they will need to find new ways to help African countries address the erosion of state institutions and governance that has made terrorism endemic across the continent.

Africa’s entanglement with terrorist and jihadi groups is hardly new. Al-Qaeda’s 1998 attacks on U.S. embassies in Dar-es-Salaam and Nairobi were planned from Sudan, where Osama bin Laden had been based between 1991 and 1996. After 9/11, security experts viewed those attacks as a crucial precursor that should have set off alarm bells. Then, in the early years of the twenty-first century, local African groups coalesced into al-Shabab, based in Somalia, which also began to pursue transnational terrorism as an affiliate of al-Qaeda. Later, al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb formed a major foothold in Mali. These developments prompted a number of Western-led antiterrorism campaigns, often supported by African forces. Most notable were the military interventions in the Sahel led by the French and other Western special forces and the initial U.S.-supported intervention force in Somalia, the so-called Somali Warlord Alliance.

But these counterterrorism operations did little to stop extremist activity in Africa. In the 2010s, countries in and close to the Sahel began to transition from being breeding grounds of terrorism to becoming the focus of terrorist attacks. Over the past few years, these countries have not only continued to be the places where terrorist groups can organize, radicalize their adherents, and spread violent extremist ideology; they also now bear the brunt of terrorist attacks and killings and the instability and breakdown in security that go with them. Worse, this activity has spread to new areas of the continent, such as Benin, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Mozambique, where there had not been jihadis previously. In these countries, terrorist groups have capitalized on long-standing popular grievances spurred by government neglect, exclusion, and poverty. The jihadi expansion has been led by new local groups with connections to al-Qaeda and its branch JNIM in the Sahel region of West Africa and to ISIS affiliates in central Africa, whose major motivations include generating wealth from illegal mining, smuggling, and transnational organized crime.

What the outside world has often failed to recognize—both in the earlier and more recent phases of extremism—are the underlying factors that have made so many African countries prone to this activity. In nearly every case, fragile or collapsing state institutions have been crucial enablers: states’ inability to ensure the welfare and security of their citizens, to exercise sovereign authority over the length and breadth of their territory, and to alleviate the widespread poverty, unemployment, and disease that have created openings for extremism. In many countries, these factors have been exacerbated by large numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees, a lack of social infrastructure, and perennial violent conflict.

The unique characteristics of African demography have added to the challenge. In contrast to the aging populations of most other regions of the world, people under the age of 30 make up nearly 70 percent of Africa’s population and are also most affected by state failure. Large numbers of young people are not in school—more than 270 million African children in 2026, accounting for more than 40 percent of the global total. Nigeria alone has nearly 20 million youth out of school, the highest of any country in the world. At the same time, youth unemployment has remained persistently high: the continental average is 18 percent, but in some countries, such as Djibouti, where mass employment opportunities are limited and young people generally lack the requisite education for skilled employment in the logistics and transport sector that dominates the economy, youth unemployment may reach more than 75 percent. Disaffected young Africans constitute a huge reservoir of potential recruits for extremist groups, which have grown commensurately: according to recent estimates, al-Shabab has more than 15,000 fighters and JNIM has around 6,000.

But state complicity also plays a role. It is now well documented that political leaders have been building ties to bandit and terrorism groups to secure and consolidate their power. For example, the emergence of Boko Haram and various other militant outfits in Nigeria has been abetted by state governors and influential politicians employing them to intimidate opponents during elections. It is worth noting, as well, that elites in Muslim-dominated northern Nigeria initially opposed the U.S. designation of Boko Haram as a terrorist group—based on the assumption that the group was defending the interests of mainstream Muslims and northerners. This kind of support helped legitimize the group and enabled it to extend its control beyond the northeast of the country. The adoption of sharia law in the early years of the twenty-first century by 12 predominantly Muslim states in northern Nigeria also helped incubate Boko Haram. In this sense, Nigeria followed the path of Sudan, whose long history of Islamic fundamentalism and practice of sharia law made it a safe haven for bin Laden as he began to build his ideology of global terrorism.

Yet another contributing factor has been climate change and natural resource wars. Many of these countries have difficult desert geographies and have been beset with growing food insecurity and conflicts over diminishing resources. The result has been the emergence of so-called ungoverned territories within a number of African countries—areas characterized by power vacuums, porous borders, and illicit mining of critical minerals and other natural resources by terrorist groups, bandits, and criminal gangs. Often in these places, parallel state structures have been established by nonstate actors—not only to provide public goods, including safety, protection, and social services but also to challenge state legitimacy through sectarian uprisings and war. As these extremist nonstate groups seek to root their ideologies in ethnic, religious, and communal identities, territorial control has become central to their goals. This is especially true of jihadi groups such as al-Shabab, Boko Haram, JNIM, and ISIS affiliates, which aim to create caliphates, although none has thus far demonstrated the capacity to take over an entire state.

Although the domestic sources of African terrorism are important, external factors and global interconnections have been even more crucial to its spread. Take the continent’s jihadi and radical Islamist movements, which have for decades been inspired and supported from outside. For example, the 1979 Iranian Revolution spurred the rise of Shiite movements among Muslim youths across Africa. The Iranian government actively supported the movements by sponsoring the establishment of schools and mosques, offering scholarships for students to study in Iran, and creating training and indoctrination programs. Today, Ibrahim al-Zakzaky’s radical Islamic Movement of Nigeria, whose goal is to overthrow the secular government and establish Islamic law, remains one of the more resilient Iranian affiliates in Africa and has training camps in northwestern Nigeria that are linked to Iran and Lebanon’s Hezbollah.

In the 1990s, the exploits of the Taliban in Afghanistan inspired young Muslim radicals in northern Nigeria, where the forerunners of Boko Haram initially called themselves the Taliban. In turn, terrorism researchers have identified Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and other Middle Eastern powers as funders of Salafi extremism, which espouses the violent imposition of Islamic law on everyone, including fellow Muslims. Such is the success of these efforts that many African terrorist groups today consider themselves part of the global network of Salafist jihadism.

Among the most important external forces driving African terrorism are porous borders and the free flows of weapons, drugs, money, and human trafficking into and out of the continent. These flows have facilitated the integration of African groups into transnational terror networks. Al-Shabab was one of the earliest examples of this phenomenon: the group was founded by Somali supporters of the Afghan mujahideen in the late 1980s. Later, it became an affiliate of al-Qaeda, pledging allegiance to the group in 2012.

Other African groups followed a similar trajectory. Al-Qaeda’s African affiliates have grown to include Ansaru, a splinter faction of Boko Haram operating in northern Nigeria, as well as al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which is based in Algeria. ISIS has added a panoply of African groups to its own network, such as Islamic State Sahel Province in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, and Islamic State West Africa Province, which is active in the Lake Chad Basin. And it has developed ties with Islamic State Central Africa Province, which also operates in parts of Mozambique and the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda; and Islamic State in Somalia, which is a rival of al-Shabab. Meanwhile, al-Shabab has cultivated links to the Houthis in Yemen, a development that has heightened the potential for transnational terrorism to become enmeshed in the struggle for control of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden between Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey following conflicts and closures in the Strait of Hormuz.

These transnational affiliations have offered African groups many advantages, bringing new sources of funding, new weapons (including drones), and training in suicide bombing and IEDs, as well as indoctrination, foreign fighters, intelligence, and logistics. In return, African terrorist groups have helped their international affiliates by engaging in sea piracy and smuggling, human trafficking and migrant smuggling, money laundering, kidnapping for ransom, robbery, livestock rustling, drug trafficking, and illegal mining. African groups use many of these activities, as well as illegally taxing the areas under their control, to raise illicit funds for their international affiliates.

In addition, African jihadis provide personnel for international operations—al-Shabab members have been involved in terrorist training operations in the Philippines—and safe havens for fugitive terrorists. During the decades of the post-9/11 war on terrorism, there was a steady influx to Africa of foreign terrorists, fighters, and instructors who were fleeing Iran, Iraq, Syria and other parts of the Middle East. Others came from North Africa, especially following the civil war in Libya and unrest in Algeria. These foreign extremists brought with them massive amounts of weapons and helped turn Africa into a center of terrorist activity. As the epicenter of global terrorism today, Africa now houses numerous al-Qaeda and ISIS operatives, a fact that increases the risk that Africa-based groups may be planning operations beyond the continent.

In theory, international engagement in African security should help contain the rising terrorism threat. But the record thus far is not promising. During the war on terrorism, the United States, the EU, the United Nations, and international security organizations provided support for numerous counterterrorism campaigns on the continent. These efforts included backing the G5 Sahel—a counterterrorism initiative by Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania, and Niger—as well as support for regional counterterrorism initiatives, including in Mozambique and Somalia, as well as the Multinational Joint Task Force, which aimed to combat terrorism in the Lake Chad region. Most of these efforts failed or were not sustained long enough to change the trajectory, and the worsening security situations that they left in their wake fueled anti-Western sentiment. And now, with Russia and China pursuing interests of their own in many parts of Africa, involvement by outside powers is often driven by a desire for strategic minerals and a quest for geopolitical influence, interventions that have only further encouraged terrorist activity.

In the Sahel, the withdrawal of U.S. and French forces between 2022 and early 2025 created power and security vacuums. Russia has quickly exploited the situation, using bilateral defense pacts and mercenary and Africa Corps forces to gain access to minerals and natural resources that France had previously controlled. Indeed, in many parts of Africa, global competition for critical minerals has become a new driver in the spread of terrorism. In the Manono district of Congo, for instance, American, Australian, and Chinese firms are enmeshed in long-running disputes over lithium deposits, which has made counterterrorism operations in the same area more difficult: the various international players no longer want to coordinate on counterterrorism and terrorist groups are using external rivalries to strengthen their own operations. A similar scenario is playing out in other resource-rich areas.

It is now urgent that leading world powers adopt a different approach. A first step is to recognize the problem for what it is. Jihadi terrorism today is not a local or regional problem afflicting a handful of African countries; it is a worldwide threat. It can be effectively tackled only through concerted and sustained international action. Although internationally-backed counterterrorism efforts by the African Union and other regional forces are more needed than ever, the new scramble for resources has become an obstacle to international collaboration in Africa. In this regard, it will be crucial to embrace the common protocols and regulatory frameworks for critical minerals and other resources being developed by the AU and other regional African organizations—which seek to reduce the scope for illicit activities and ensure that that the countries benefit more from the resources through more inclusive and accountable governance structures.

Most important, outside powers need to engage with the root causes that have made the continent so prone to terrorist activity, even when it has been effectively countered elsewhere in the world. As the former UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said in 2015, “Good governance is what will kill terrorism.” Northern Ireland after the Good Friday Agreement—whose institutional reforms such as power sharing, human rights protections, and community policing proved to be more effective than military operations—is a case in point; so is the 2016 peace agreement between the Colombian government and the FARC, which included governance reforms in previously neglected parts of the country as part of its stabilization measures.

The United States as well as governments in Europe and international bodies need to shift their focus from military operations to addressing the actual social and economic sources of state fragility that have made so many African countries fertile ground for conflict and extremist violence. This would of course involve strengthening state capacities, and it would require regional efforts as well as more targeted development assistance. None of it will be easy, but doing nothing would be far worse. Unless African countries and their international partners can begin to address the underlying dynamics that are driving Africa’s transnational terrorism problem, it is unlikely to stay in Africa for much longer.

#5923. Florida AG subpoenas DSA over potential illegal funding from Cuba and China

The AG’s office is examining whether the Democratic Socialists of America took contributions from ‘foreign sources of concern.’ (Credit: @AGJamesUthmeier).

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office issued an investigative subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to investigate whether the organization accepted contributions from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China.

"Our laws prohibit accepting contributions from foreign sources of concern," Uthmeier said in a video statement. "We will not allow foreign adversaries to influence Florida through the backdoor of non-private fundraising."

The subpoena demands documents related to recent DSA delegations to China and Cuba, where organization members met with Cuban government officials, to determine if the DSA violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, according to Uthmeier.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA ACTIVISTS SIGNED PLEDGE TO SUPPORT, DEFEND 'CHINESE SOCIALISM'

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued a subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America to determine whether the organization accepted donations from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China. (Getty Images)

Uthmeier did not detail specific criminal allegations or name individuals accused of violating state law.

The DSA has repeatedly praised the Cuban regime and routinely advocates for lifting American sanctions and ending the U.S. embargo against Havana.

The legal action comes shortly after several DSA-backed candidates won races across federal, state, and local levels in last week's elections.

#5919. The Luxury of Children

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

JESÚS FERNÁNDEZ-VILLAVERDE is Howard Marks Presidential Professor of Economics at the University of Pennsylvania. This piece is adapted from “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World,” co-authored with Patrick Norrick and forthcoming in the 2027 Annual Review of Economics.

Why the Baby Bust Is Making the World More Unequal

The world’s fertility crisis is more severe than is commonly understood. Last year, humanity’s total fertility level dropped below what demographers call the replacement rate—that is, the average number of children that a woman must have to keep a population constant over the long run. This has never happened before. There have been periods when the human population declined because of wars or epidemics, such as the Black Death, in the fourteenth century, or the diseases brought by Europeans to the Americas in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. But now, simply as a function of their choices, humans will see the world population peak around 2055 and then begin to fall.

The story of the coming decades is not simply one of dwindling and aging. There is a great deal of variation in the baby bust. The most surprising trend may be one that has overturned basic assumptions about fertility rates. Where once it was thought that people—and, by extension, countries—with higher levels of income and education would have lower fertility rates than those who were poorer and less educated, the inverse is increasingly true. Many wealthier people and countries boast higher fertility rates than many poor people and countries.

The inversion is revealing of why governments have had a hard time coming to grips with the fertility crash. The best explanation for why people are no longer having babies is that child-rearing at the scale necessary to maintain populations is fundamentally at odds with the structures of modern life and modern societies. Once an economic necessity, children are now an economic luxury. That portends a world in which economic inequality is accentuated by demographic inequality, with widening fissures within countries and among them. The whole world is grappling with a decline in fertility, but in many different ways. And those differences will stoke further divisions, tensions, and even conflict.

Humanity falling below replacement has passed largely unnoticed. The central projections in the latest release of the United Nations World Population Prospects (in 2024), known as the report’s “medium variant,” still places the world’s total fertility rate slightly above replacement in 2026 and expects the global population to peak as late as 2084. But this medium variant does not fully incorporate the recent drops in births recorded by national statistical agencies, and its projections for future fertility rest on questionable assumptions, including forecasting a strong recovery of fertility rates in countries such as China. By comparison, the report’s “low variant” (the forecast that takes a more pessimistic view of future fertility) accords nearly exactly with my own assessment, which reflects more recent national statistics and takes a less optimistic view on the possible recovery of fertility. In that reading, the world has dropped below replacement fertility levels (approximately 2.2 children per woman) and will only keep dropping.

Fertility rates are plunging so fast that they are overturning many assumptions about demography. The steepest fertility declines have occurred in unexpected countries. Consider this test. Pick the state with the highest fertility rate among the following: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Jamaica, Iran, Malaysia, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, Sri Lanka, and the United States.

The United States, the wealthiest of the 12, has the highest fertility rate. This holds true even when just assessing the fertility rate of mothers born in the United States (immigrant mothers have a slightly higher fertility rate than native mothers). Dozens of other middle-income countries now have fertility levels below that of the United States.

That trend runs against the old explanation for demographic change, which held that fertility invariably falls as a community or society gets richer. That is demonstrably no longer the case. Among the countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), richer members tend to have higher fertility rates than do poorer ones, even after controlling for migration flows. Take Mexico. According to the most recent survey, in 2024, a Mexican woman could expect to have 1.2 children over her lifetime, well below the 1.57 average of non-Hispanic white women in the United States. Mexico’s income per capita is only about 28 percent of the U.S. level. And just two decades ago, fertility rates in Mexico were much higher than those in the United States.

This dynamic obtains not just among countries but also within them. Richer and more educated households in the United States and other advanced economies now tend to have more children than poorer and less educated ones, reversing a pattern that had held for centuries.

There is no single, simple answer for why this has happened. Most theories do not hold up against international evidence. Factors that seem to contribute to lower fertility in the United States, for instance, such as higher housing prices, don’t seem to matter elsewhere, as many countries have seen even steeper fertility declines without skyrocketing housing prices.

Or take another favorite culprit, smartphones. Some researchers have suggested that the spread of the smartphone stoked atomization and a desire for individual fulfillment, discouraging many people from having children. But fertility rates have been plunging worldwide since the late 1960s, well before smartphones appeared, and there is little evidence of an acceleration in the drop after their introduction. Instead, the device is more likely an accelerator of underlying mechanisms than a cause in itself: by my calculations, smartphones compressed into ten years a change in fertility that would have occurred anyway over 25.

Another common explanation for drops in fertility is the spread of female education and employment. Freed from the domestic function of birthing and raising babies, the argument goes, women have chosen to prioritize other goals instead of child rearing. Although that shift may indeed have played a role in the twentieth century in lowering fertility rates, it is no longer so clearly causal today. Indeed, across OECD countries, the correlation between fertility, on the one hand, and female education and employment, on the other, is positive: the countries where women are more educated and more likely to work outside the home are also the countries with higher fertility rates. And in other regions for which demographers have good vital statistics, such as Latin America, the women not having children in 2026 are the least educated and the ones most likely to not be part of the workforce.

In the absence of neat, definitive explanations, a broader explanation for the global fertility crash comes into view. As societies embrace what is often termed “modernity,” they become incapable of maintaining replacement-level fertility rates. Modernity describes how countries have organized contemporary life around formal institutions (such as schools, universities, and health systems), specialized expertise (through degree accreditation, standardized exams, and professional licensing), and large-scale systems of coordination (such as multinational corporations, governments, and global supply chains). It is not synonymous with capitalism; communist countries, too, invested heavily in mass education and bureaucracies (and saw concomitant declines in fertility). The only way to run large, complex societies that harness modern technology at scale is to standardize knowledge and detach it from local custom through mass education, systems of expertise, and bureaucracies.

Modernity raises the cost of children and lowers the cost of childlessness. Parents must equip children with formal knowledge and credentials, an endeavor that takes decades of effort and spending. Tight career schedules also conflict with parents’ biological clocks. The most productive years for a research economist, for example, are usually between 30 and 45. Those are also the years when one needs to spend the most time with children. No matter how much accommodation a university offers, the day still has only 24 hours. Even when a researcher manages to produce both a large family and strong academic output, one can always wonder how much more that researcher would have produced with a smaller family.

And modernity has also made it easier not to have children. In traditional agrarian and artisan economies, children were useful factors of production, helping in the fields and workshops. Children also provided parents and other older relatives with eldercare. But the modern organization of economic life no longer requires children to perform those roles and the advent of welfare states has given the elderly other forms of support. Lineage once determined people’s present and future; it no longer does so in such a comprehensive way.

There are some exceptions to this seemingly universal trend. Tight-knit religious communities, such as the ultra-Orthodox in Israel and the Amish in the United States, have managed to maintain high fertility rates well above replacement level. But these groups have also stayed apart from much of modern life. For example, the Amish live in rural areas, where housing is much cheaper, and they end formal education at eighth grade, which eliminates one of the main costs of raising a child in a modern society, advanced education.

Apart from these idiosyncratic pockets, modernity has spread around the planet, with fertility falling everywhere. But rates are tumbling unevenly. In 1980, the richer an OECD country, the fewer children its women had. By 2000, the opposite was beginning to become true. The same reversal shows up inside countries. In Sweden, the demographer Martin Kolk has found that in every cohort born between 1940 and 1970, men with higher lifetime incomes have more children, and that among women born since the 1960s, the poorest have the fewest children. In the United States, the economists Moshe Hazan and Hosny Zoabi have found that in the first decade of the twenty-first century, women with a graduate degree had about 2.0 children, significantly more than the 1.8 for women who stopped at a bachelor’s degree.

Many adults still want to have children and flourishing families. When Gallup asked Americans about their ideal number of children in July 2025, the average answer was 2.7, a figure that has barely changed since the 1970s. But children are costly and bring no income. They have become something of a luxury good that richer people can afford more of than poorer people can. In the same way that a richer household owns, on average, a more expensive car than a poorer one, it also has more children—at least since the 1990s. Prosperous parents can hire help at home, order prepared meals, pay for premium grocery delivery or laundry services, and afford tuition and tutoring.

Richer families (and, among them, the most educated parents) also have more stable family lives. For instance, among Americans born between 1957 and 1964 (a cohort whose adult lives can be observed almost in full), about half of men with a high school diploma but no college education had seen their first marriage end in divorce by age 55, compared with 27 percent of men with a bachelor’s degree or more. Stable families lead to higher fertility (and much better outcomes for the children). In short, income and education soften some of the worst consequences of modernity. The intuition of this result applies, as well, to countries as a whole: richer countries can, on average, afford more “luxuries,” including children, than poorer countries.

If the modernity conjecture is right, the flip in the correlation between income and fertility that is evident within OECD countries will extend to all other countries over the next few decades. This is already happening in the Americas: among countries with at least 20 million inhabitants, the United States has the highest fertility rate in the hemisphere, well ahead of Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, and Mexico, and matched only by Peru, whose fertility rate is plummeting fast. (Venezuela’s official fertility rate is pure fiction.)

The same phenomenon will occur in sub-Saharan Africa over the next few decades. It is often projected that the continent’s high fertility rates will make up for shortfalls elsewhere—but that will likely not happen. Indeed, in those sub-Saharan African countries for which demographers have slightly better statistical data, fertility rates are dropping very quickly. For example, a recent household survey in the Republic of Congo has shown a decrease in fertility from 5.1 children per woman in 2011–12 to 3.5 in 2025. Similar falls are happening elsewhere and likely to accelerate as sub-Saharan Africa succumbs to the same factors that have sped fertility declines elsewhere.

The coming years will produce deep changes in populations within countries and across countries. The already sharp divide between regions and social groups with higher average incomes and education levels and those with lower average incomes and education levels will grow more pronounced, with the added dimension of contrasting fertility rates. The school district of a wealthy suburb outside a major East Coast city may not need to grapple with the widespread school closings that urban districts are already experiencing. And since political power in a democracy follows, at least to some extent, the number of voters, these different regions and social groups will see their relative influence in American politics change: New York, for instance, has lost 19 votes in the electoral college since the 1940s.

Something similar can happen among countries. In 1972, nearly eight times as many children were born in China as in the United States. In 2025, that figure has dropped to 2.2 times as many. China’s total fertility rate in 2025 was 0.93, while the U.S. rate was 1.58. If fertility rates remain at those levels, the United States will overtake China in annual births at some point in the 2080s and in total population by around 2120. That date might arrive earlier if the gap between the fertility rates of China and the United States continues to widen.

Demography is not necessarily destiny, but a world in which the United States has a larger population than China is very different from the world today. The shrinking and aging of populations will have first-order effects on a country’s economic performance. In research with Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao, I have documented that nearly all of Japan’s poor economic performance relative to the United States since 1990 can be explained by its worse demographics, not by financial crises or poor economic policy. Among the great powers, the United States is the least exposed to demographic headwinds. Younger populations tend to be more innovative and less reliant on public support, a fact that bodes well for American prospects in the competition to come.

But for most other countries, demographic decline will produce significant problems. Aging Japan, for instance, is likely the best-case scenario for countries reaching a demographic sunset. It boasts a capable state and a homogeneous society with a high degree of consensus. More important, Japan became rich before it got old. Countries such as Mexico and Thailand, which lack many of Japan’s advantages, may struggle to weather the same demographic headwinds. While rich economies can rely on immigration to soften some of the effects of falling fertility, countries such as Tunisia or Bolivia, which lose many people to emigration, may find it harder to deal with their own baby busts. The new dynamics of fertility augur a world in which gaps between the haves and the have-nots grow even wider, as poorer countries and communities endure strains that wealthier countries and communities manage to escape.

Short of an unlikely turn to the social mores of deeply conservative and ideological communities, such as the Amish, only transformations in material circumstances will help raise fertility rates. Governments have had a hard time determining how to tackle fertility decline. Policy can do only so much in convincing people to make the monumental decision to have children. But that does not mean that governments should not try to reverse these trends. Their policies should respect the freedom of citizens to form the families they believe are best for them. Ultralow fertility seems to be caused not by a lack of desire for children but by the absence of the conditions that would make having children easier, or even possible.

In this vein, some policies are no-brainers. Governments should make education systems more accessible and less competitive than, for example, the ones found in East Asia and in the United States, where high levels of cost and stress discourage having children. They should build more affordable housing and provide more affordable childcare. Such material changes may have only a marginal impact on rates, but even, for instance, raising the U.S. total fertility rate to 1.7 from the current 1.58 would produce a significant impact. Fertility rates behave like the rates of return on a retirement fund: small yearly differences accumulate into large differences over time. Policies that give people greater material freedom to have children can thus be very consequential in the long term.

If governments fail to enact these policies, and if, indeed, these policies fail to encourage a broader rise in fertility, the world will simply become more unequal. Richer families and richer countries will gain greater weight in the population, while poorer families and poorer countries dwindle and weaken. These shifts will create political tensions, as shrinking populations will add to their relative poverty the desperate sense that they have no demographic future. Eastern Germany offers a preview. Since reunification, its young people (above all, its young women) have left for western Germany, its towns have emptied and aged, and its voters have turned to the parties at both extremes of the political spectrum. Many countries in the world are about to become eastern Germany, but few of them will have a western Germany to pay the bills. Demographers often suggest that the world is united by the crash in fertility rates. In truth, demographic decline will likely divide the world even further.
